title: Aluminum branch wiring
hook: From 1965 to the mid-1970s, some houses were wired with solid aluminum instead of copper, and CPSC found that connections in pre-1972 aluminum-wired homes were 55 times more likely to reach fire-hazard conditions.
summary: Single-strand aluminum wire was used for ordinary outlet and light circuits in an estimated two million homes and mobile homes built from 1965 on, according to CPSC. The risk is at the connections, at outlets, switches and splices, which can loosen and overheat. CPSC recognizes specific permanent repairs.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: CPSC estimated in 1974 that about two million homes and mobile homes had been built with aluminum wiring since 1965. No figure gives the share of houses of the era.

check: Look at any exposed cable in the attic, basement or near the panel for 'AL' or 'ALUMINUM' printed on the plastic jacket every few feet.
'CU-clad' or 'copper-clad' aluminum is a different, lower-risk product.
Warning signs: cover plates that feel warm, flickering lights, or a smell of burning plastic at an outlet.
Do not open outlet or switch boxes yourself.
action: Call a licensed electrician who uses the CPSC-recognized repairs: rewiring with copper, COPALUM crimp connectors, or AlumiConn connectors. CPSC calls CO/ALR outlets and switches an incomplete repair and twist-on pigtail connectors a temporary measure. If you notice warm plates or a burning smell, stop using that circuit until it is checked.

sources.quote: homes built before 1972, and wired with aluminum, are 55 times more likely to have one or more wire connections at outlets reach “Fire Hazard Conditions”
An estimated two million homes and mobile homes have been constructed using aluminum wiring since 1965.
Between approximately 1965 and 1973, single-strand (solid) aluminum wiring was sometimes substituted for copper branch-circuit wiring in residential electrical systems

caveat: CPSC's hazard figure covers homes wired before 1972; later aluminum wire used an improved alloy and has less data behind it. CPSC dates use only to 'the mid 1970s', so the end year is soft. Most houses of the era were wired in copper.

title: Asbestos-cement siding and shingles
hook: Hard, thin cement shingles with a wood-grain or dimpled face were a popular siding for much of the 20th century, and many contain asbestos.
summary: Asbestos-cement siding and roof shingles came into use soon after 1907, and CPSC lists them as a household asbestos source. They are low risk when intact and painted, and release fibers when sawn, drilled or broken.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. It was one of several competing sidings, and many installs were re-siding jobs on older houses.

check: Look at the siding: hard, thin shingles, often 12 by 24 inches, with a wavy or straight bottom edge and a pressed wood-grain or dimpled surface.
They crack or chip rather than dent, and show nail heads at the bottom corners.
Check under later vinyl or aluminum siding, where they are often hidden.
Some look-alikes were made without asbestos, so only a lab test confirms it.
action: Keep them painted and intact. Replace broken pieces with non-asbestos fiber-cement look-alikes, or side over them. Full removal should follow asbestos work rules.

sources.publisher: US CPSC, Asbestos In The Home
sources.quote: Some roofing and siding shingles are made of asbestos cement.
Asbestos cement first came into use as an exterior cladding after 1907, when Austrian engineer Ludwid Hatschek came up with a way to shape the material into sheets

caveat: No source gives a firm end year; manufacturers stopped at different times. Many installs were re-siding jobs on older houses, so build year predicts this poorly.

title: Asbestos floor tile and sheet flooring
hook: Old 9-inch-square floor tiles and the black glue under them frequently contain asbestos, and there was no effective federal ban on asbestos floor tile until a 2019 rule.
summary: Vinyl and asphalt floor tiles, the backing on sheet vinyl, and the adhesive used to lay them frequently contained asbestos through much of the 20th century. EPA's 1989 ban was overturned in 1991, leaving vinyl-asbestos tile unbanned until a 2019 rule. Intact flooring is low risk; sanding, grinding or breaking it up releases fibers.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Resilient flooring was very common in mid-century kitchens, baths and basements, and many but not all products contained asbestos.

check: Look under carpet, in basements and closets, and under newer floor layers for old tiles. 9 by 9 inch tiles are the strongest clue; 12 by 12 also occur.
Black, tar-like 'cutback' adhesive under old tile often contains asbestos too.
Sheet flooring with a gray or white felt-like backing from before the mid-1980s is suspect.
Only a lab test confirms it.
action: The most common approach is to leave it in place and cover it with new flooring. Never sand it. If it has to come up, test first and use a licensed abatement contractor.

sources.publisher: US CPSC, Asbestos In The Home
sources.quote: RESILIENT FLOOR TILES (vinyl asbestos, asphalt, and rubber), the backing on VINYL SHEET FLOORING, and ADHESIVES used for installing floor tile.

sources.publisher: US EPA, EPA Actions to Protect the Public from Exposure to Asbestos
sources.quote: As a result, the 1989 asbestos regulation only bans new uses of asbestos in products that would be initiated for the first time after 1989 and bans 5 other specific product types.
Vinyl tiles manufactured in the 20th century frequently contain asbestos fibers, which are today referred to as Vinyl-Asbestos Tiles (VAT).

caveat: Install years come from inspector references, not an agency, and manufacturers stopped at different times. Many tiles of the era contain no asbestos.

title: Asbestos in drywall joint compound
hook: Drywall joint and patching compound could contain asbestos until CPSC banned it in 1978, and you cannot tell by looking.
summary: CPSC banned consumer patching and tape joint compounds containing asbestos, effective in early 1978, along with textured paints that contained it. Before that, some major brands contained asbestos and others did not. It is a concern when walls are sanded, cut or demolished.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Several major brands contained asbestos and several did not.

check: This cannot be seen. Any drywalled or refinished wall or ceiling from before about 1980 is a candidate.
Before sanding or demolition, have a lab test the joint compound layer itself, not just the board.
action: Leave intact walls alone. Test before renovating; if it is positive, use a licensed abatement contractor or your state's approved wet methods for the affected areas.

sources.quote: troduced into commerce after January ... 16, 1978, are banned hazardous products. ... are banned hazardous products after ... June 11, 1978.
Products such as spackling compounds, tape joint compounds, and other mixtures that consumers use to patch or seal cracks, holes, or other imperfections in drywall and other surfaces.

sources.publisher: US CPSC, Asbestos In The Home
sources.quote: Asbestos may be present in textured paint and in patching compounds used on wall and ceiling joints. Their use was banned in 1977.

sources.publisher: US EPA, EPA Actions to Protect the Public from Exposure to Asbestos
sources.quote: In 1977, the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) banned the use of asbestos in artificial fireplace embers and wall patching compounds.

caveat: The ban covered consumer products, so contractor stock and already-purchased material may have been used for a while after 1978. The start year is approximate, tied to the spread of drywall after World War II.

title: Asbestos pipe and boiler insulation
hook: CPSC says houses built between 1930 and 1950 may have asbestos insulation, often as white wrap on heating pipes and boilers in the basement.
summary: Asbestos was widely used to insulate steam and hot-water pipes, boilers and ducts. EPA banned installing asbestos pipe and block insulation on boilers, tanks and pipes in 1975. Damaged wrap can shed fibers into the basement and, through ducts, into living space.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. It depends on whether the house still has an original steam or hot-water system, and much of this insulation has already been removed or sealed.

check: In the basement or crawl space, look for white or gray wrap on pipes that looks like corrugated cardboard in cross-section.
Look for a hard white plaster-like coating on pipe elbows, boilers and tanks.
Check duct seams and the edges of registers for white paper or cloth tape.
Do not touch frayed material; only a lab test confirms asbestos.
action: If it is in good condition, a professional can seal and wrap it. If it is damaged, or before you replace a boiler or finish a basement, have it tested and handled by a licensed abatement contractor.

sources.publisher: US CPSC, Asbestos In The Home
sources.quote: Houses built between 1930 and 1950 may have asbestos as insulation.

sources.publisher: US EPA, EPA Actions to Protect the Public from Exposure to Asbestos
sources.quote: In 1975, EPA banned installation of asbestos pipe insulation and asbestos block insulation on facility components, such as boilers and hot water tanks
voted unanimously to grant a petition to ban commercial asbestos paper that is sold to consumers or installed in consumers' homes

caveat: Asbestos duct tape and paper were used later than pipe wrap and have no clear end date. Many houses of this era have had this insulation removed or sealed.

title: Asbestos in popcorn ceilings
hook: Bumpy 'popcorn' ceilings put up from the 1950s into the 1980s sometimes contain asbestos, and only a lab test can tell.
summary: EPA banned spray-applied asbestos for insulation in 1973 and for other uses in 1978, which reached decorative ceiling texture. Existing stock was exempt, so asbestos texture may be found in ceilings applied through the 1980s. Not every popcorn ceiling contains asbestos; it is a concern mainly when scraped, sanded or water-damaged.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of popcorn ceilings or of how many contain asbestos.

check: Look up: a bumpy, cottage-cheese-like sprayed texture, sometimes with glitter, is the type to ask about.
You cannot see asbestos. A small sample has to go to an accredited lab (PLM analysis).
Do not scrape a sample dry; many state and local air agencies publish homeowner sampling instructions.
action: If it is intact, leaving it alone is usually best, as CPSC advises for asbestos in good condition. Test before you remove or disturb it; if it is positive, it can be sealed, covered with new drywall, or removed wet by a licensed abatement contractor.

sources.publisher: US EPA, EPA Actions to Protect the Public from Exposure to Asbestos
sources.quote: In 1978, EPA banned spray-applied surfacing materials for purposes not already banned.

sources.publisher: US CPSC, Asbestos In The Home
sources.quote: SOUNDPROOFING OR DECORATIVE MATERIAL sprayed on walls and ceilings. Loose, crumbly, or water-damaged material may release fibers.
existing inventories of asbestos-bearing texturing materials were exempt from the ban, so it is possible to find asbestos in popcorn ceilings that were applied through the 1980s

caveat: The 1950 start and the 1980s tail are approximate; no primary source gives residential install years. A ceiling re-textured later may differ from the age of the house.

title: Atlas Chalet and Stratford shingles
hook: Atlas Chalet and Stratford shingles, sold from at least 1998 until 2010, drew a federal lawsuit, but class certification was denied, so there is no settlement.
summary: Atlas developed these overlay shingles in the 1990s and discontinued them in 2010, according to a federal court. Owners sued over the shingles, and in 2017 the court denied class certification. They are reported to be common in the Southeast, especially around Atlanta.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. They are described as common on Atlanta-area houses of 1999 to 2010 and rare elsewhere, but without data.

check: Look at the roof from the ground: they resemble three-tab shingles with a darker printed shadow band across each tab.
Look for small pock-like blisters and bald spots.
Roofers in the Southeast tend to recognize them on sight.
action: Have a roofer look if you see blistering. With no settlement, replacement is at the owner's cost unless an insurer accepts a storm claim, and because they are discontinued, matching repairs is difficult.

sources.publisher: US District Court, N.D. Georgia, Dishman v. Atlas Roofing Corp. (MDL 2495), Opinion and Order filed 8 June 2018 (govinfo)
sources.quote: In 2010, the Defendant discontinued sales of the Shingles.
The Defendant developed the Shingles in the 1990s as a line of “overlay” products

sources.publisher: US District Court, N.D. Georgia, Dishman v. Atlas Roofing Corp., Opinion and Order filed 9 June 2017 (govinfo)
sources.quote: The Plaintiffs and putative class members are purchasers of Atlas Chalet and Stratford Shingles

caveat: The first year of sale is uncertain; the court says only 'in the 1990s'. Many roofs from this period have been replaced, and most houses of the era have other shingles.

title: Balloon framing
hook: In many older two-story houses the wall cavities run unbroken from the basement to the attic, which lets a fire climb inside the walls.
summary: Balloon framing, with studs running the full height of the house and floors hung from them, was common until the late 1940s, when platform framing took over. The open cavities act like chimneys in a fire. Adding fireblocking at the top and bottom of each cavity is the usual fix.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Inspectors generally assume balloon framing in two-story wood-frame houses built before about 1920; one-story houses are effectively unaffected.

check: In the basement, look up where the floor joists meet the outside wall: open stud cavities rising past the joists, with no flat wooden plate on top, mean balloon framing.
In the attic, look down between the studs at the eaves for open cavities.
At the second floor, joists nailed to the sides of studs and resting on a board let into the studs are the giveaway.
action: Have a contractor add fireblocking (lumber, mineral wool or dense-packed insulation) at the basement and attic ends of each stud cavity where they can be reached.

sources.quote: Balloon framing using a technique suspending floors from the walls was common until the late 1940s, but since that time, platform framing has become the predominant form of house construction.
The first building clearly using balloon framing was a warehouse constructed in 1832 in Chicago
where a cavity may traverse multiple floors

caveat: The end date varies: sources put it from the late 1940s to the mid-1950s, and timing differed by region and builder. Many houses of the 1930s and 1940s are platform framed.

title: Bosch and Siemens dishwashers (2009 recall)
hook: Some Bosch and Siemens built-in dishwashers made from 1999 to 2005 have a part that can overheat and start a fire.
summary: BSH recalled about 476,500 Bosch and Siemens dishwashers made from May 1999 to July 2005 and sold through December 2006. An electrical component can overheat, and CPSC had 51 reports including 30 fires. These were common builder and remodel choices at the time.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 476,500 units were recalled; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Check the brand on the front control panel: Bosch or Siemens.
Open the door and find the model and serial number label on the upper right edge of the inner door.
Bosch models SHE43C, SHE44C, SHE46C, SHE56C, SHU33, SHU42, SHU432, SHU43C and SHU53A, and Siemens SL34A, are on the list. Compare the serial number with the range on the CPSC notice.
action: If it matches, stop using it and contact BSH as the 2009 notice directs; check the notice for whether the free repair is still offered. A dishwasher this old may be due for replacement anyway.

sources.quote: certain Bosch® and Siemens® dishwashers manufactured from May 1999 through July 2005
About 476,500
from May 1999 through December 2006 for between $550 and $1,100

caveat: Many dishwashers from these years have since been replaced. A house built in this window is the likeliest to still have an original one.

title: Built before mandatory airtightness testing (2012 energy code)
hook: The 2012 energy code was the first to make new houses pass a whole-house air leakage test.
summary: The 2012 International Energy Conservation Code added a mandatory whole-house pressure (blower-door) test, a stricter duct leakage test and more insulation, and DOE put it at about 30 percent more efficient than the 2006 code. A house built before its state adopted the 2012 code was not held to that test, so it likely leaks more air.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Houses built before their state adopted the 2012 code were not required to pass this test. Adoption dates by state were not researched.

check: Look near the electrical panel or furnace for an energy code certificate or a posted blower-door test result.
Ask the seller or builder whether a blower-door test or energy rating was done.
Notice drafts around outlets, attic hatches, recessed lights and window trim on a cold or windy day.
action: Nothing is required. If the house feels drafty or bills are high, an energy audit with a blower-door test shows where air sealing would help most.

sources.quote: Mandatory whole-house pressure test
~30% better than 2006 IECC
In the US, the IECC of 2012 adopted whole building airtightness requirements, including mandatory testing.

caveat: This is a model code. States and cities adopted it at different times and some much later or not at all, so the end year here is stretched a few years and is soft. Check your state's adoption date.

title: Built before energy codes
hook: The first US energy standard for buildings, ASHRAE 90, was published in 1975, so a house built before then was not built to any energy code.
summary: Before energy codes, insulation levels, window types and air sealing were up to the builder. Model codes followed from 1975, but states adopted them on their own schedules, some a decade or more later. Many older houses have had insulation added since.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of how many older houses have been upgraded. A house built before 1975 was built without any energy code.

check: Look in the attic at the depth of insulation between and over the joists.
Check the windows: hold a light to the glass; one reflection means single pane, two close reflections mean double.
action: An energy audit shows where the house loses heat. Air sealing and attic insulation usually come first, then wall insulation.

sources.quote: The original standard, ASHRAE 90, was published in 1975.
is a building code created by the International Code Council in 2000
In 1994, BOCA, SBCCI, and ICBO merged to form the International Code Council (ICC)

caveat: 1975 is when the first voluntary standard was published, not when your state enforced one; some states lagged by a decade or more, and a few still have no statewide residential energy code. Later code dates were not confirmed.

title: Cadet and Encore wall heaters
hook: More than 1.9 million Cadet and Encore in-wall electric heaters, sold mainly in the Northwest and California from about 1978 to 2000, were recalled as a fire hazard.
summary: CPSC announced the recall in 2000; a later reminder cited four deaths, two serious burn injuries and six house fires. The heaters were sold mainly in California, Idaho, Montana, Oregon and Washington. Houses heated with electric wall heaters often have several.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: CPSC: more than 1.9 million units, concentrated in five states. No figure gives the share of houses; it applies mainly to houses with electric wall heat.

check: Look through the grille of each electric wall heater for the label on the front of the heater assembly; do not take anything apart.
Recalled models start with FW, FX, LX, TK, ZA, Z, RA, RK, RLX, RX, RW or ZC followed by three digits.
The brand will be Cadet or Encore.
action: Stop using any recalled heater and replace it with a current model. The recall remedy was not found to be still running, so contact Cadet to ask before paying for replacements.

sources.quote: announced today the recall of more than 1.9 million Cadet and Encore brand in-wall electric heaters, distributed mainly in California, Idaho, Montana, Oregon and Washington
sold and distributed primarily in California, Idaho, Montana, Oregon, and Washington from about 1978 through 2000
These heaters have been installed in homes from 1985 through 1992 in Oregon, Washington, California, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming.

caveat: CPSC gives the sale years only as 'about' 1978 through 2000, and only the listed model prefixes are affected. Heaters were also fitted as replacements in older houses.

title: Arsenic-treated (CCA) deck lumber
hook: Pressure-treated wood in decks and play sets built before 2004 was commonly treated with an arsenic compound, and EPA says never to burn it.
summary: Wood treated with chromated copper arsenate (CCA) was used for residential decks and playsets until manufacturers stopped making it for homeowner uses at the end of 2003. Arsenic can rub off on hands and leach into the soil underneath. EPA does not recommend removing existing structures.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. EPA says CCA-treated wood was used in decks and playsets before 2004, but no market-share figure was found.

check: Look at decks, play sets, fences and garden edging built of pressure-treated wood before 2004.
End tags or ink stamps may read 'CCA' with a number such as 0.40; newer wood reads ACQ, CA or MCA.
Arsenic swab test kits and lab tests exist.
action: Wash hands after contact, never burn the wood or use it for garden beds, and wear a mask when cutting it. Sealants may reduce surface arsenic, but CPSC testing found few held up after two years. Replace with alternative-treated wood or composite when the deck is due.

sources.quote: In December 2003, chromated arsenicals manufacturers voluntarily discontinued manufacturing chromated arsenicals-treated wood products for homeowner uses.

sources.publisher: US CPSC staff report on surface coatings for CCA wood
sources.quote: cancel the registration of CCA for use in wood for most residential structures (e.g., playgrounds, decks, picnic tables, etc.) after December 30, 2003
EPA does not believe there is any reason to remove or replace CCA-treated structures, including decks or playground equipment.

sources.publisher: Federal Register, 68 FR 17366, 9 April 2003, EPA notice of cancellation order for CCA residential uses (govinfo)
sources.quote: Effective December 31, 2003, this product
Timber treated before that date was still allowed to be sold, but retailers were required provide warning labels.

caveat: Old stock could still be sold after 2003, so some 2004 decks used it, and the 1975 start is approximate. Decks are often built or replaced long after the house, so the deck's age matters more than the house's.

title: Central, Gem and Star O-ring sprinkler heads (2001 recall)
hook: If a house from around 1990 to 2001 has fire sprinklers, some heads from that era were recalled because they may not open in a fire.
summary: About 35 million O-ring sprinkler heads made by Central Sprinkler, sold under the Central, Gem and Star names, were recalled in 2001 because corrosion or contaminants in the water can stop them working. They were installed in houses as well as larger buildings. The free replacement program ended on August 31, 2007.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: NIST said fewer than 5 percent of US homes had sprinklers in 2011, so few houses of this age have any sprinkler heads at all.

check: First check whether the house has sprinklers: small heads on ceilings or high on walls.
Look at the frame or deflector of each head for 'CENTRAL', 'STAR', the letters 'CSC', a 'G' in a triangle, or a star-shaped symbol.
Compare any model or date stamped on the head with the CPSC model list.
action: The free replacement program closed on August 31, 2007, so any affected heads would need replacing at your own cost. Have a fire sprinkler contractor confirm and replace them.

sources.quote: with O-rings from 1989 until 2000 that are covered by this program
The sprinklers were installed nationwide in a wide variety of buildings, including houses, apartments, hospitals
postmarked by August 31, 2007

caveat: Dry-type heads in this recall go back to the mid-1970s, but these are rare in houses. Most houses of this era have no sprinklers, so this only matters if yours does.

title: CertainTeed organic shingles
hook: CertainTeed estimated that about 1.86 million buildings got its felt-based organic shingles between 1987 and 2005, and a class settlement followed.
summary: CertainTeed organic shingles (sold as Hallmark Shangle, Horizon, Independence, Custom Sealdon and others) were made from July 1987 through 2005 and covered by a 2010 class settlement. They were sold mainly in the upper Midwest. This matters only if the original roof is still on the house.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CertainTeed's own estimate in court: about 1,857,000 structures in the US and Canada were built with these shingles from 1987 to 2005, a small share of roofs laid in those years.

check: Look for the brand names Hallmark Shangle, Horizon, Independence or Custom Sealdon on wrappers, invoices or warranty papers.
A torn shingle shows a brown or black felt core rather than white glass fibers.
Heavy curling at tab corners and blistering on an old roof are typical of organic shingles.
action: If the roof is failing, re-roof. Contact CertainTeed to ask whether claims are still possible; the claim deadline could not be confirmed.

sources.publisher: US District Court, E.D. Pennsylvania, In re CertainTeed Corp. Roofing Shingle Products Liability Litigation (MDL 1817), Opinion filed 31 August 2010 (govinfo)
sources.quote: CertainTeed estimates that, from 1987 to 2005, approximately 1,857,000 structures were built using CertainTeed organic shingles.
CertainTeed denies that the shingles were faulty, but quit manufacturing that particular type in 2005.

caveat: Many roofs from this period have already been replaced, and the older the house, the less likely the original roof survives. Installation could trail manufacture by a year or so.

title: Challenger breaker panels
hook: Challenger panels, the successor to the Zinsco line, were sold from 1978 to 1994, and one batch of their GFCI breakers was recalled in 1988.
summary: The Zinsco product line was relabeled Challenger in 1978, and the business passed to Eaton in 1994. In 1988 CPSC announced a recall of about 9,000 Challenger GFCI breakers, types HAGF-15 and HAGF-20, made between February 22 and April 29, 1988, which might not provide ground-fault protection. Broader overheating claims about Challenger panels rest on inspector reports, not an agency finding.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. The 1988 recall covered about 9,000 breakers.

check: Look for 'Challenger' embossed on the panel door handle or printed on the label inside the door.
Look for 15- or 20-amp breakers with a test button marked HAGF-15 or HAGF-20; those are the recalled types.
action: Have an electrician check the panel for heat damage and for HAGF breakers. If either turns up, or your insurer asks, replacing the panel is the usual route.

sources.quote: These type HAGF-15 and type HAGF-20 circuit breakers were manufactured between February 22, 1988 and April 29, 1988
There are no recalls on these panelboards, with the exception of approximately 1,000 Eaton/Cutler-Hammer panels in 2014 that were built on the Challenger design.
In 1978, the line changed names again, and was re-labeled Challenger.

caveat: Panels labeled Challenger from 1978 to about 1981 are Zinsco-design panels. Production years come from one reference article, and the recall covered only breakers made in a two-month window in 1988.

title: Chlordane termite treatment
hook: From 1948 to 1988, chlordane was a standard termite treatment around foundations, and ATSDR says more than 50 million people have lived in treated homes.
summary: Chlordane was applied to the soil around and under houses to stop termites; from 1983 that was its only approved use, and EPA banned all uses in 1988. It lingers for years, with higher levels in basements and crawl spaces. ATSDR says houses built since 1988 have not been treated with it.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: ATSDR: over 50 million people have lived in chlordane-treated homes; Wikipedia puts it at about 30 million homes. Use was heaviest in the deep South and Southwest.

check: There is no visible sign. Look for old termite-treatment records or pest-control stickers.
Look for patched drill holes in the slab, garage floor or along the foundation walls.
Only an indoor air or soil lab test confirms it.
action: If you are concerned, test the indoor air. Seal slab cracks and crawl-space and duct leaks, ventilate basements and crawl spaces, and avoid growing food crops right beside the foundation.

sources.quote: From 1948 to 1988 chlordane was used in the United States as a pesticide on agricultural crops, lawns, gardens, and homes.
the EPA banned all uses of chlordane in 1983 except to control termites. In 1988, EPA banned all uses.

sources.publisher: ATSDR Public Health Statement for Chlordane
sources.quote: Over 50 million persons have lived in chlordane-
chlordane was used for termite-treatment of approximately 30 million homes until it was banned in 1988

caveat: Treatment was done both during construction and later on existing houses, so any house standing before 1988 in termite country may have been treated. Many houses never were.

title: Cloth-covered rubber-insulated wiring
hook: Between knob-and-tube and modern plastic cable, houses were wired with rubber-insulated wire in a woven cloth jacket, and that rubber crumbles with age.
summary: Cable of this kind was invented in 1922 and first listed in the National Electrical Code in 1926. For decades after, wiring commonly used rubber-insulated conductors inside a cloth or steel-armored jacket. The rubber dries out and flakes, worst at hot ceiling light boxes, and most of this cable has no ground wire.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. For a house built from about 1930 to 1955 that was never rewired, this was the normal wiring method.

check: At the panel, in the basement or in the attic, look for cables with a braided fabric outer covering (black, silver or brown, sometimes tarry) instead of smooth plastic.
Inside boxes, the individual wires have cloth over black or red rubber that cracks or flakes. Ceiling light boxes, where heat damage is worst, are the place for an electrician to look first.
Do not bend or flex old wires to test them.
action: Have an electrician check the lighting circuits and any brittle runs. Replacing the worst runs, or rewiring, is the usual fix; GFCI or AFCI protection can be added in the meantime.

sources.quote: NM was first listed and described in the NEC in 1926, but it was invented a few years earlier by the Rome Wire Company in 1922 in Rome, New York

caveat: The start is anchored by the 1926 code listing, but the end year is a rule of thumb, not a confirmed date: plastic-insulated cable took over gradually, roughly by the 1960s. Many houses of this era have since been rewired.

title: Coaire and Quietside tankless water heaters (2014 recall, no remedy)
hook: These tankless water heaters sold from 2008 to 2014 can overheat, and the maker is gone, so there is no fix on offer.
summary: About 29,000 Coaire and Quietside S-Line condensing tankless gas water heaters sold from July 2008 to August 2014 can overheat and start a fire. CPSC had 40 overheating reports. The firm is out of business and no remedy is available.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 29,000 units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for a white wall-mounted tankless heater about 25 to 28 inches tall.
Check for 'S-Line Condensing' on the top front.
Check for the brand 'Coaire' or 'Quietside' on the bottom front.
action: If it matches, stop using it and have it replaced. CPSC says the firm is no longer in business and a remedy is no longer available.

sources.quote: About 29,000 in the United States and 2,200 in Canada
from July 2008 through August 2014 for between $500 and $2,000
The firm is no longer in business. A remedy is no longer available.

caveat: Tankless heaters are often installed as replacements, so one could be in a house of any age.

title: Consolidated (Premier) attic furnaces
hook: Between 1983 and 1994, Consolidated Industries built well over 100,000 horizontal furnaces for California homes under many brand names, and CPSC tied them to about 50 fires.
summary: Consolidated Industries built horizontal gas furnaces with 'NOx rods' to meet California air rules and sold them under many brand names. CPSC warned about them in 2000 and announced a recall in 2001, citing about 50 fires. The company is out of business, so there is no remedy today.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC put production at about 140,000 units (2001) or 190,000 (2000), all for California, with about 50 fires reported. Most are now past normal furnace life, and no count of survivors exists.

check: Look at the furnace in the attic or crawl space for steel rods mounted above the burners (the 'NOx rods'); every one of these furnaces has them.
Check the label for Consolidated, Premier, Addison or Weatherking, or private labels including Amana, Bard, Carrier, Goettl, Goodman, Janitrol, Comfort-Aire, Trane and American Standard.
CPSC's notice lists the affected model numbers.
action: If you find one, replace the furnace; the maker is gone and no recall remedy remains. Until then, CPSC suggested an ionization smoke alarm in the attic as an interim measure.

sources.quote: manufactured approximately 140,000 of these furnaces for sale in California between 1983 and 1994 under many different brand names
Consolidated manufactured approximately 190,000 of these furnaces from 1983 through 1994 under many different brand names.

caveat: These furnaces went only to California, and most furnaces of these years are other makes. A replacement furnace installed in an older house during these years could also be one.

title: Counterfeit Square D circuit breakers (mid-2000s recalls)
hook: In the mid-2000s fake breakers labeled Square D were sold through distributors, and they may not trip on an overload.
summary: Square D determined that breakers sold as QO and QOB by some distributors were counterfeit and can fail to trip when overloaded, a fire hazard. One recall alone, through Specialty Lamp International, covered about 371,000 breakers sold from May 2005 to June 2006. Other distributors had similar recalls.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 371,000 units were recalled by one distributor, and other recalls add more; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Open the panel door and look for black breakers labeled Square D QO or QOB.
On genuine breakers (except some made before 2003) the amp rating is written in white paint on the handle.
Ask an electrician to check the hidden signs: a Square D insignia molded on the side and a yellow chromate mounting clip.
action: If a breaker looks wrong, have an electrician replace it. The distributor named in the recall notice may offer inspection and replacement or a refund.

sources.quote: have been determined by Square D to be counterfeit and can fail to trip when they are overloaded, posing a fire hazard to consumers
May 2005 through June 2006 for between $3 and $23

caveat: Only one of several counterfeit recalls was confirmed for this guide, so the years here are approximate. Breakers are swapped in panels of any age.

title: Engineered I-joist floors
hook: By 2005 about half of new wood floors were built on engineered I-joists, which perform well day to day but can fail quickly in a fire if left exposed.
summary: I-joists, invented in 1969, have a thin OSB or plywood web between small top and bottom flanges. Their known drawback is very rapid failure when directly exposed to fire, which matters over an unfinished basement or garage with no ceiling. Covering the underside with drywall is the usual protection.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Wikipedia: about 50% of wood light-frame floors used I-joists as of 2005.

check: Look up at the basement or garage ceiling for I-shaped joists: a thin OSB or plywood web with small lumber flanges top and bottom.
They are usually printed with a brand such as TJI, BCI or LPI.
If you can see them, they are unprotected from below.
action: Consider covering exposed I-joists with 1/2-inch drywall, and make sure working smoke alarms cover every level, including the basement.

sources.quote: Invented in 1969, the I-joist is an engineered wood product that has great strength in relation to its size and weight.
As of 2005, approximately 50% of all wood light framed floors used I-joists.

caveat: A model-code requirement to cover them was reportedly added around 2012, but that was not confirmed and states adopted it unevenly. The hazard applies only where the joists are exposed.

title: Factory-built roof trusses
hook: If your attic is a web of diagonal 2x4s joined by toothed metal plates, the roof is built from factory trusses, and cutting even one can badly weaken it.
summary: Metal-plate-connected roof trusses date from the mid-1950s and became a common way to frame roofs. They are efficient, but every piece carries load. Cutting or altering a truss, for attic storage, a skylight or ductwork, needs an engineer's repair design.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists for houses by year built.

check: In the attic, look for diagonal 2x4s forming W or M shapes, joined by toothed galvanized steel plates, usually 24 inches apart.
Rafters, by contrast, are larger boards running from the ridge to the wall with open space between.
Look for cut or notched members and plates that have backed out of the wood.
action: Nothing is needed unless trusses are damaged or altered. Before any attic conversion, skylight or other change that touches a truss, get an engineer's design.

sources.quote: John Calvin Jureit invented the truss connector plate and patented it in 1955.

caveat: Truss use grew over decades, and many houses still use rafters, especially custom homes and complex roofs. Sources date the connector plate to 1952 or 1955.

title: Federal Pacific Stab-Lok panels
hook: Federal Pacific Stab-Lok breaker panels, made from 1950 to 1980, are among the panels home inspectors flag most, and CPSC's own testing found breakers that failed calibration tests.
summary: Federal Pacific Electric made Stab-Lok breakers from 1950 to 1980, and they turn up mostly in houses built before 1990. CPSC investigated from 1980 to 1983, confirmed breakers failing UL calibration tests, then closed the matter without a recall and without deciding whether they are safe. CPSC advises having these panels inspected by an electrician.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Claims of 'millions of homes' come from advocacy sources, and no market-share data was found.

check: Open the panel door (not the inner cover) and read the label for 'Federal Pacific Electric', 'FPE' or 'Federal Pioneer'.
Look for 'Stab-Lok' printed on or near the breakers.
Breaker handles often have a red or orange stripe across the tip.
action: Have a licensed electrician inspect it, as CPSC advises. Replacing the whole panel is the usual fix; replacement breakers of the same type are not shown to be any better. There was never a recall, so there is no manufacturer remedy.

sources.quote: the Commission closed the matter without making a determination as to the safety of FPE circuit breakers or the accuracy of the manufacturer’s position on the matter
Stab-Lok is a brand name of electrical circuit breakers that were manufactured primarily by Federal Pacific Electric from 1950 to 1980.

caveat: CPSC closed its investigation without a finding either way, and the widely quoted failure rates come from independent testing that could not be checked. FPE's own production ended around 1980; later panels of this design came from successor companies.

title: Florida home built before the statewide wind code
hook: Florida homes permitted before March 1, 2002 were built to local codes rather than the statewide Florida Building Code that followed Hurricane Andrew.
summary: After Hurricane Andrew, South Florida created High-Velocity Hurricane Zones in its 1994 code, and the statewide Florida Building Code took effect March 1, 2002. Older homes may have roofs held to the walls only by nails rather than metal straps, and no protection over windows and doors. A wind-mitigation inspection documents what a house actually has.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Wikipedia: about 4.7 million Florida homes predate the modern Florida Building Code.

check: In the attic at the eaves, look where each truss or rafter meets the top of the wall.
Only angled nails means toe-nailed; a small metal bracket is a clip; a metal strap wrapping over the truss is a wrap, and two straps a double wrap.
Check windows and doors for impact-rated labels or shutter hardware.
Your county permit record gives the original permit date.
action: Get a wind-mitigation inspection by a licensed inspector; it records these features for your insurer. Upgrades such as roof-to-wall straps, re-nailing the roof deck and shutters are usually done at re-roofing time.

sources.publisher: Wikipedia (Effects of Hurricane Andrew in Florida)
sources.quote: The Florida Building Code was established in 1998 and put into effect by 2002.
no homes built after the unified Florida Building Code (FBC) was adopted March 1, 2002 were destroyed
The 1994 South Florida Building Code created High-Velocity Hurricane Zones (HVHZ) and each subsequent major hurricane prompted specific changes to the code.

caveat: What counts is the permit application date, not the year the house was finished, so 2002 houses can go either way. In Miami-Dade and Broward the stricter code dates from 1994. Many pre-2002 homes do have clips or straps.

title: Fuse box and 60-amp service
hook: Houses built from 1940 through 1965 commonly got a 60-amp fuse box with four screw-in fuses; after 1965, 100-amp service became the norm.
summary: A 60-amp fuse box was typical in houses built from 1940 through 1965, after which 100-amp panels became common. The risks are over-fusing (a bigger fuse on a small circuit, which defeats the protection) and a service too small for modern loads. Many have been upgraded, but nobody counts how many.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Most fused services of this era have probably been upgraded, but no data shows the share.

check: Find the main panel: round screw-in fuses, or pull-out blocks holding cartridge fuses, instead of rows of switches mean a fuse box.
The service size is printed on the main pull-out or main fuse; look for '60'.
A round meter base outside usually indicates 60 amps or less.
action: Have a licensed electrician check that each fuse matches its wire size and assess the service. Upgrading to a 100- to 200-amp breaker service, which involves the utility, is the usual long-term fix. Never fit a larger fuse to stop one blowing.

sources.quote: A common design of fuse box that was featured in homes built from 1940 through 1965 was the 60-amp fuse box that included four plug fuses

caveat: The 1940 to 1965 range comes from one reference source, and the code history of the 100-amp minimum was not confirmed. Many houses of this era have had their service upgraded.

title: Galvanized steel water pipes
hook: Gray, threaded galvanized steel was common for water pipes until the 1950s, and it rusts from the inside, slowly choking the flow.
summary: Galvanized steel supply pipe was common in houses until the 1950s. It corrodes inside, which brings low pressure, rusty water and leaks at threaded joints. EPA counts galvanized service lines that could have picked up lead from upstream pipe as lead service lines.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists for galvanized pipe inside houses. EPA estimated about 2.8 million standalone galvanized service lines in 2023.

check: Look at exposed pipe in the basement, crawl space or at the water heater: dull gray, with threaded fittings.
A magnet sticks to it, and a scratch shows silver-gray steel, not copper color.
Symptoms: low pressure on upper floors, rusty water after the taps sit unused, rust stains at joints.
action: Have a plumber assess it. Repiping the house in copper or PEX is the usual remedy, because replacing sections tends not to last. If the service line is galvanized, check the utility's inventory for lead upstream.

sources.quote: There are also an estimated 2.8 million standalone galvanized service lines.
Galvanized pipes requiring replacement (GRR)—or pipes made from galvanized steel, which lead can adhere to. These pipes are also considered lead service lines.
Galvanized steel was common until the 1950s; the pipes rust inside and out.

caveat: Sources disagree by more than a decade on when galvanized stopped being used, and none is a code history. Many houses of this age have been repiped.

title: Garage door opener without auto-reverse
hook: Garage door openers made before 1991 did not have to reverse when they hit something, and photo-eyes or similar protection became required on openers made from 1993.
summary: CPSC reported 54 children killed since 1982 after being trapped under doors with automatic openers. Federal law required openers made from January 1, 1991 to reverse on contact, and openers made from January 1, 1993 to add protection such as photo-eye sensors. It is the opener's age that matters, not the house's.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of pre-1993 openers still in use.

check: Look for two small sensor 'eyes' about 6 inches off the floor on each side of the garage door opening.
Check the date on the opener's label.
Test it: lay a 2x4 flat on the floor under the door; the door should reverse when it touches the board.
action: If the opener does not reverse or has no sensors, replace it with a current UL 325-compliant unit rather than trying to retrofit it. Until then, keep children clear of the door while it moves.

sources.quote: The legislation also requires that residential garage door openers manufactured on or after January 1, 1993 comply with additional entrapment protection requirements developed by UL.

sources.publisher: 16 CFR Part 1211 (2023 edition, via govinfo; ecfr.gov refuses automated requests)
sources.quote: This standard applies to all residential garage door operators manufactured on or after January 1, 1993 for sale in the United States.

all automatic residential garage door openers manufactured on or after January 1, 1991 must conform to the entrapment protection requirements of the Underwriters Laboratories (UL) Standard for Safety, UL 325
A requirement for redundant entrapment-prevention devices was added in 1993

caveat: The 1993 rule can be met by a constant-contact wall button instead of photo-eyes, so a newer opener without eyes is possible. Openers are often added or replaced long after a house is built.

title: Gas water heaters made before 2003 (no flammable-vapor protection)
hook: Gas tank water heaters made since July 2003 are built so gasoline fumes on the floor can't reach the flame; older ones are not.
summary: Under an industry standard developed with CPSC, standard gas tank water heaters made after July 1, 2003 have a flame arrestor that stops spilled gasoline or solvent vapors from igniting. CPSC said vapor ignition by gas water heaters was involved in nearly 800 home fires a year. An older heater still in service lacks this protection.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: Any gas tank heater made before July 2003 lacks it. Many heaters that old have been replaced; no count of how many remain exists.

check: Check whether the water heater is a gas tank model (a burner at the bottom and a vent pipe on top).
Read the label for the words 'Flammable Vapor Ignition Resistant' or 'FVIR'.
Look for the manufacture date in the label or serial number: after July 2003 means it should have the protection.
Notice whether gasoline, paint thinner or solvents are stored near it, especially in a garage.
action: Keep gasoline and solvents well away from any gas appliance. If the heater predates the standard, plan to replace it with a current model.

sources.quote: calls for conventional tank-type gas water heaters manufactured after July 1, 2003, to be equipped with new safety technology
Gas water heater ignition of flammable vapors is involved in nearly 800 residential fires
Residential combustion water heaters manufactured since 2003 in the United States have been redesigned to resist ignition of flammable vapors

caveat: This was a voluntary industry standard, not a federal law, and it covers standard 30, 40 and 50 gallon gas tank heaters. Water heaters are replaced often, so the heater's own date matters far more than the house's.

title: Gravity ('octopus') furnace
hook: Some older basements still hold a huge round 'octopus' furnace with fat ducts reaching upward, and its duct wrap may contain asbestos.
summary: Gravity furnaces, installed from the late 1800s to the mid-20th century, move heat without a blower through large sloping ducts. InterNACHI says only about half their heat reaches the house. The ducts were often wrapped in material that may contain asbestos.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of how many remain; most have been replaced.

check: In the basement, look for a very large round or boxy furnace with several large sheet-metal ducts sloping up from the top and no blower compartment.
White or gray cloth-like or corrugated-paper wrap on the ducts may be asbestos; do not disturb it.
action: Plan for replacement: have any duct wrap tested and removed by a licensed asbestos abatement contractor, then install a modern furnace and ducts. InterNACHI advises buyers to negotiate the price to cover this.

sources.quote: These antiquated furnaces were installed from the late 1800s to the mid-20th century and are still found in use in some older buildings.

caveat: The date range stands in for InterNACHI's 'late 1800s to the mid-20th century'. Most of these furnaces have long since been replaced.

title: Gree-made dehumidifiers (2013 recall)
hook: About 2.5 million dehumidifiers sold under a dozen familiar brands from 2005 to 2013 can overheat and catch fire.
summary: Gree made dehumidifiers sold as Danby, De'Longhi, Fedders, Frigidaire, Kenmore, SoleusAir, GE and others between 2005 and 2013. They can overheat, smoke and catch fire. A 2016 reannouncement cited about 450 fires, and many of these units ran unattended in basements.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 2.2 million units were recalled in the US in 2013, rising to about 2.5 million with the GE-brand expansion; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look in the basement, crawlspace entry and laundry area for a portable dehumidifier.
Read the brand and pint capacity on the front.
Find the sticker with the model number and date code on the back, front or side of the unit.
Compare the model and date code with the tables on the CPSC recall notice. Many Gree and SoleusAir models are listed as all units.
action: If it matches, unplug it and stop using it. The remedy was a refund from Gree, not a repair; check the recall notice for whether refunds are still offered.

sources.quote: About 2.2 million in the United States and 52,500 in Canada
from January 2005 through August 2013 for between $110 and $400
This recall was expanded on January 30, 2014 to include 350,000 GE-brand dehumidifiers made by Gree.
The model number and date code are printed on a sticker on the back, front or side of the unit.

caveat: A dehumidifier is a portable appliance, so it may have come with the house or been bought later for a house of any age. A separate 2023 Gree recall covers other models made 2011 to 2014.

title: Gree-made dehumidifiers (2023 recall, made 2011-2014)
hook: A second Gree dehumidifier recall in 2023 covered models that the 2013 list missed.
summary: In 2023 Gree recalled about 1.56 million dehumidifiers from 42 models sold as Kenmore, GE, SoleusAir, Norpole and Seabreeze, made from January 2011 to February 2014. They can overheat and catch fire. If you checked a unit against the 2013 list only, it is worth checking again.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 1.56 million units were recalled; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for a portable dehumidifier in the basement, crawlspace entry or laundry area.
Check the brand: Kenmore, GE, SoleusAir, Norpole or Seabreeze.
Read the model number on the unit's label and compare it with the 42 models on the 2023 CPSC notice (for example Kenmore 407.53530310 or GE ADEH50LPQ1).
action: If it matches, unplug it and stop using it. The notice offers a refund from Gree; check the notice for current details.

sources.quote: This recall involves 42 models of dehumidifiers with brand names Kenmore, GE, SoleusAir, Norpole and Seabreeze, manufactured between January 2011 and February 2014.
starting in 2011 through 2014 for between $110 and $400.

caveat: This is a portable appliance that owners buy for houses of any age, so build year is only a rough guide. The 2023 and 2013 recall lists are separate, and one unit may need checking against both.

title: Hardboard siding (Masonite and others)
hook: Hardboard siding swells and rots when water gets in, and in 1996 a jury found Masonite's siding defective.
summary: Hardboard is a pressed wood-fiber siding, smooth or embossed, that was common on houses of the 1980s and 1990s. InterNACHI notes it can rot and swells more than natural wood when wet. In 1996 International Paper lost a class action brought by owners whose Masonite siding had deteriorated.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Class counsel described a Masonite class of about 4 million homeowners, but that figure could not be confirmed.

check: Look at cut ends or where paint has failed: smooth or embossed board of uniform brown fiber, with no visible strands or plies.
Check bottom edges, butt joints and around nails for swelling, 'mushroomed' nail heads and soft spots.
action: Keep paint and caulk in good shape, replace damaged boards, or re-side when damage spreads. No open claim program was found.

sources.publisher: InterNACHI, How to Inspect the Exterior (2012)
sources.quote: Hardboard can be affected by moisture. It can rot. It swells more than natural wood when it is wet.
In 1996, International Paper (IP) lost a class action suit brought by homeowners whose Masonite siding had deteriorated. The jury found that IP's Masonite siding was defective.

caveat: The 1980 to 1998 range is the reported Masonite class window, which could not be confirmed, and hardboard was used before 1980 too. Brands look alike; identifying one needs the marks on the back of a board.

title: High-flow toilets and showerheads
hook: Most toilets made before 1994 use more than twice the water of the 1.6-gallon models required since.
summary: Under the Energy Policy Act of 1992, toilets made from 1994 can use no more than 1.6 gallons per flush, and showerheads no more than 2.5 gallons per minute. A house built before 1994 that still has its original fixtures uses more water. Nothing here is unsafe; it is a water bill question.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Toilets and showerheads are replaced often, so many older houses already have newer ones.

check: Lift the toilet tank lid: the gallons per flush is usually stamped or printed inside the tank, or on the bowl behind the seat, with a manufacture date.
'1.6 gpf / 6.0 Lpf' or lower means it meets the 1994 rule.
No marking and a large tank suggest a pre-1994 toilet.
action: If you want lower water bills, replace with a WaterSense-labeled toilet and showerhead, and check whether your utility offers a rebate.

sources.publisher: US House Subcommittee on Energy and Power, hearing on H.R. 623, 27 July 1999, Serial No. 106-76 (GovInfo)
sources.quote: Since 1994, new toilets manufactured in the United States can only use 1.6 gallons of water per flush and showerheads are permitted to use only 2.5 gallons of water per minute.
less water than the current federal standard of 1.6 gallons per flush
This law went into effect on January 1, 1994, for residential buildings and January 1, 1997, for commercial buildings.

caveat: The rule applied to fixtures made from January 1, 1994, so houses finished in 1994 may still have older stock. Fixtures are swapped so often that build year predicts this poorly.

title: Home fire sprinklers
hook: California has required fire sprinklers in new one- and two-family homes since 2011, so newer California houses generally have small sprinkler heads in the ceilings.
summary: A model code change requiring sprinklers in new one- and two-family homes took effect January 1, 2011. California adopted it statewide; Pennsylvania adopted it and repealed it the same year. Sprinklers need little care, but painted or blocked heads must be replaced and the control valve must stay open.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: California has required sprinklers in all new residential construction since 2011 (Wikipedia). Outside places that require them, they are uncommon in houses.

check: Look up: small sprinkler heads, often under flat white cover plates, in the ceiling of every room.
Find the riser, a pipe with a gauge and flow switch, near the water main or in the garage.
action: Keep the control valve open and never paint over a sprinkler head. Replace any head that has been painted or blocked.

sources.publisher: NIST (publication abstract: The Economics of Residential Fire Sprinklers and the Potential Impact of Recent Code Changes)
sources.quote: a change to the International Residential Code requiring sprinklers in all new one- and two-family homes, which became effective January 1, 2011
In 2011, Pennsylvania and California became the first US states to require sprinkler systems in all new residential construction.

caveat: Some cities outside California also require sprinklers by local ordinance. Houses permitted before 2011 but finished later may not have them.

title: House not bolted to its foundation
hook: Many older West Coast houses on crawl spaces are not adequately bolted to their foundations, and in a strong earthquake they can slide off.
summary: Older wood-frame houses on raised foundations often have the wooden sill plate sitting on the concrete without enough anchor bolts, and short 'cripple' walls with no bracing. In strong shaking the house can shift off its foundation. Bolting the sill and sheathing the cripple walls with plywood is the standard retrofit.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Only houses on raised foundations with crawl spaces are affected; slab houses are not.

check: Go into the crawl space and look along the top of the concrete foundation at the wooden sill plate.
Bolts with nuts and washers every 4 to 6 feet mean it is bolted.
If there is a short wood-stud wall between the foundation and the floor, check whether plywood or OSB is nailed to its inside face.
Houses on a concrete slab have no cripple wall.
action: A contractor can bolt the sill and brace the cripple walls following your state's or city's prescriptive retrofit plans; taller cripple walls need an engineer. In California, check whether a state grant program covers your ZIP code.

sources.quote: additional requirements that were developed following observations from earthquakes, particularly the 1994 Northridge earthquake in California, where extensive sill plate splitting led to significant structural damage

in many structures built before 1950 the sill plate that sits between the concrete foundation and the floor diaphragm (perimeter foundation) or studwall (slab foundation) may not be sufficiently bolted in

caveat: There is no single code year: a reference source says many houses built before 1950 lack adequate bolting, and the pre-1980 cutoff used in California is a grant-program screen, not a code date. Many houses have already been retrofitted.

title: Kidde dual-sensor smoke alarms with a yellow cap (2018 recall)
hook: A yellow cap left on at the factory can block one of the two sensors in some Kidde alarms from 2016 and 2017.
summary: Kidde recalled about 452,000 dual-sensor smoke alarms, the hard-wired PI2010 and battery-powered PI9010, with date codes from September 10, 2016 to October 13, 2017. A yellow cap left on during manufacture can cover one sensor, so the alarm may not detect smoke properly. You can see the cap through a side opening.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 452,000 units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for alarms with 'KIDDE' printed on the front.
Take one down and read the model (PI2010 or PI9010) and date code on the back.
If the date code is between 2016 Sep. 10 and 2017 Oct. 13, look through the side opening for a yellow cap.
action: If it matches, contact Kidde for the free replacement listed in the notice, and check the notice for current details.

sources.quote: A yellow cap left on during the manufacturing process can cover one of the two smoke sensors
About 452,000 in the U.S.
from September 2016 through January 2018 for between $20 and $40

caveat: The PI9010 is a battery model and both were sold as replacements, so these turn up in houses of any age, not just ones built in 2016 to 2018.

title: Kidde hard-wired smoke alarms (2014 recall)
hook: Some hard-wired Kidde alarms sold in 2014 may not sound after a power outage.
summary: Kidde recalled about 1.2 million hard-wired smoke and smoke/CO alarms, models i12010S, i12010SCO and KN-COSM-IBA, made between October 2013 and May 2014 and sold from January to July 2014. They can fail to alert to fire or carbon monoxide after the power goes out and comes back.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 1.2 million units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for white round alarms 5 to 6 inches across with 'Kidde' engraved on the front.
Twist one off its base and read the model number and manufacture date on the back.
Recalled: i12010S made Dec 18, 2013 to May 13, 2014; i12010SCO made Dec 30, 2013 to May 13, 2014; KN-COSM-IBA made Oct 22, 2013 to May 13, 2014.
The i12010S and i12010SCO have sealed batteries; the KN-COSM-IBA has a front compartment for AA backup batteries.
action: If it matches, contact Kidde for the free replacement offered in the 2014 notice. Check the notice for whether it is still available.

sources.quote: Kidde residential smoke alarm model i12010S with manufacture dates between December 18, 2013 and May 13, 2014
About 1.2 million in the United States and about 112,000 in Canada
from January 2014 through July 2014 for between $30 and $50

caveat: These alarms also went into older houses as replacements, and a 2014 house may have had its alarms changed since. The label is what counts.

title: Kidde NightHawk hard-wired smoke/CO alarms (2016 recall)
hook: A popular hard-wired smoke and CO alarm from 2004 to 2010 can go quiet at the end of its life, so it seems fine when it is not.
summary: Kidde recalled about 3.6 million NightHawk talking combination smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, model KN-COSM-IB, made from June 2004 to December 2010. If the batteries are replaced near the alarm's seven-year end of life, it can stop giving its end-of-life chirp and stop protecting the home. They were sold through electrical distributors and home centers, so builders used them.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 3.6 million units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for white round alarms 5 to 6 inches across with 'Kidde' engraved on the front.
Twist one off its ceiling base (it stays wired to a plug) and read the label on the back.
Look for model KN-COSM-IB with a manufacture date between June 1, 2004 and December 31, 2010.
A compartment on the back for a 9-volt backup battery is another sign of this model.
action: If it matches, contact Kidde about a replacement and check the recall notice for whether the offer is still open. Any alarm made in these years is well past its stated life, so replace it either way.

sources.quote: Kidde NightHawk talking combo smoke/CO alarm with model number KN-COSM-IB and manufacture dates between June 1, 2004 and December 31, 2010.
from June 2004 through December 2010 for between $40 and $65

caveat: No one knows how many went into new houses versus replacement installs. Alarms get swapped over the years, so read the label rather than going by build year.

title: Kidde plastic-handle fire extinguishers (2017 recall)
hook: Kidde recalled about 37.8 million fire extinguishers because some may not spray when you need them.
summary: In 2017 Kidde recalled 134 plastic-handle extinguisher models made from 1973 to August 2017, plus eight push-button Pindicator models made from 1995 to September 2017. They can clog, need too much force to work, or lose their nozzle. CPSC reported one death and about 16 injuries.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 37.8 million units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look under the kitchen sink, in the pantry, garage and utility room for any Kidde extinguisher.
Note whether it has a plastic handle (red, white or silver models) or a push-button Pindicator top.
Read the model number on the label and compare it with the model list on the CPSC recall notice.
On units made in 2007 or later, a 10-digit date code is printed on the side of the cylinder near the bottom.
action: If the model is on the list, replace it and contact Kidde through the product safety recall page on kidde.com. Check the recall notice for whether the replacement offer is still open.

sources.quote: The recall involves 134 models of Kidde fire extinguishers manufactured between January 1, 1973 and August 15, 2017
About 37.8 million (in addition, 2.7 million in Canada and 6,730 in Mexico)

caveat: Extinguishers are bought, not built in, so the year a house was built predicts little: owners add them to houses of every age. The recall did not cover every Kidde extinguisher, only the listed models.

title: Kidde TruSense smoke alarms (2021 recall)
hook: Some Kidde TruSense alarms sold in 2019 and 2020 can fail to alert to a fire.
summary: Kidde recalled about 226,000 TruSense smoke and combination smoke/CO alarms sold from May 2019 to September 2020 because they can fail to alert to fire. Only alarms with the TruSense logo are included.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 226,000 units were recalled; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for the TruSense logo or the words 'AMBER=FAULT' printed on the front of each alarm.
Take it down and read the model number on the back.
Recalled models: 2040-DSR, 2050-DS10, 2060-ASR, 2070-VDSCR, 2070-VASCR, 2070-VDSR and 2070-VASR.
action: If it matches, contact Kidde for the free replacement alarm. Check the recall notice for current details.

sources.quote: Only alarms with the TruSense logo
from May 2019 through September 2020 for between $10 and $70

caveat: These were sold as replacements as well as for new houses, so check the label in a house of any age.

title: Kitec plumbing
hook: Kitec plumbing, often bright orange and blue pipe with brass fittings, was recalled by its maker in 2005 because the fittings corrode quickly.
summary: Kitec is a PEX-aluminum-PEX pipe system from IPEX, widely installed in the western US from the early 1990s. Its high-zinc brass fittings lose zinc and corrode, causing leaks and reduced flow. IPEX recalled the fittings in 2005.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: InterNACHI counts at least 60,000 homes in southern Nevada and New Mexico from lawsuits filed, and says tens of thousands more are likely in parts of Arizona, California and Texas. Nationally it is rare.

check: Look at the water heater, under sinks and at any manifold: Kitec pipe is usually bright orange (hot) and bright blue (cold).
Read the print on the pipe for Kitec or sister names such as PlumbBetter, IPEX AQUA, WarmRite or Kitec XPA.
Brass fittings are stamped 'Kitec' or 'KTC'.
Some houses have a warning sticker inside the electrical panel door.
action: If you find it, talk to a plumber about replacing it; a full repipe is the usual fix. No open compensation program was found.

sources.quote: Kitec® is a brand of brass plumbing fitting that was recalled in 2005 by its manufacturer, IPEX, due to its tendency to quickly corrode. The fitting was widely installed throughout the western United States since the early 1990s.

The Kitec system, a PEX-Aluminum-PEX composite pipe product formerly sold in Canada, was discontinued following widespread premature failures primarily caused by the dezincification of its brass fittings, leading to leaks and property damage.

caveat: The 1995 to 2007 window is the commonly quoted one; InterNACHI says it was in use from the early 1990s, and the end year is unconfirmed. It is concentrated in a few western markets, and most houses of the era never had it.

title: Knob-and-tube wiring
hook: Houses wired before about 1940 started out with single wires strung on porcelain knobs, no ground wire, and insulation that is now more than 80 years old.
summary: Knob-and-tube was the standard way to wire a house from about 1880 into the 1940s: separate cloth-covered wires run on ceramic knobs and through ceramic tubes, with no ground. The insulation gets brittle with age, and the US Department of Energy says active knob-and-tube should be replaced before insulation is added around it. Many houses were only partly rewired, so old runs can survive in walls and attics.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. A house wired between about 1900 and 1930 almost certainly started with it; how much is still live depends on later rewiring, which nobody tracks.

check: In the unfinished basement ceiling or the attic, look for white ceramic knobs nailed to the joists and ceramic tubes passing through them.
Look for two separate cloth-covered wires running several inches apart, rather than one plastic-sheathed cable.
Supporting clues: push-button light switches, two-slot outlets and a fuse box.
Modern cable at the panel does not rule it out, because knob-and-tube is often spliced in further along the circuit.
action: Have a licensed electrician find out which circuits are still live, especially before adding insulation, and keep insulation off any live runs. Replacing those circuits is the usual fix. Talk to your insurer early: InterNACHI notes that many insurers refuse to cover active knob-and-tube.

sources.publisher: US Department of Energy, Building Technologies Program, "Energy Renovations: Insulation" guide
sources.quote: For fire safety, active knob-and-tube wiring should be replaced before your contractor begins the insulation project.
in common use in North America from about 1880 to the 1940s
It was common in North America and Japan starting in the 1880s, remaining prevalent until the 1940s in North America

caveat: Sources put the end of new installs anywhere from about 1930 (DOE) to the 1940s (trade and reference sources), so the end date is soft. Many houses of this age have been fully or partly rewired.

title: Lead paint
hook: EPA says 87% of homes built before 1940 have some lead-based paint, and lead paint for homes was banned only in 1978.
summary: Paint made after February 27, 1978 for homes is limited to 0.06% lead. Lead paint is mainly a hazard when it chips or chalks, or is disturbed by sanding and renovation, which makes dust that harms young children. Federal law requires sellers of pre-1978 homes to disclose known lead paint and give buyers a 10-day window to test.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: EPA: 87% of homes built before 1940 and 24% of homes built from 1960 to 1978 have some lead-based paint. HUD's national survey found it in 34.6 million homes, 29.4% of all US housing.

check: You cannot identify lead paint by sight; it takes an XRF test by a certified inspector or a lab paint-chip test.
The most likely places are original windows, doors, trim, porches and exterior siding.
Warning signs are many layers of old paint, a cracked 'alligator' pattern, or chalking.
action: If young children live in the house or you plan to renovate, get a lead inspection or risk assessment. Contractors working on pre-1978 homes must follow EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule. Options range from stabilizing and repainting to abatement by certified firms; do not dry-sand or scrape old paint yourself.

sources.publisher: US EPA, Lead-Based Paint Program Frequent Questions (January 12, 2026)
sources.quote: 87% of homes built before 1940 have some lead- based paint, while 24% of homes built between 1960 and 1978 have some lead-based paint.

sources.publisher: US EPA, Lead-Based Paint Program Frequent Questions (January 12, 2026), citing HUD AHHS II
sources.quote: estimated that 34.6 million homes (29.4% of all housing units) in the United States contain lead-based paint that was applied before the residential use of lead-based paint was banned in 1978.
manufactured after February 27, 1978,
Until now, the maximum level of lead allowed in consumer paints has been 0.5 percent. CPSC has lowered this amount to 0.06 percent

caveat: Paint made before the ban could still be applied in 1978 and a little later. Most houses built from 1960 to 1978 do not have lead paint; the share is far higher in older houses.

title: Lead water service line
hook: The pipe that brings water from the street into many older houses is made of lead, and EPA estimates about 4 million of these lines are still in use.
summary: Lead service lines were common in older cities and were banned for new installations in June 1986. EPA says lead pipes are more likely in older cities and in homes built before 1986, though a trade source says lead was rarely used for service pipe after about 1950. Your water utility's public service line inventory is the best way to find out.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: EPA's 2025 estimate is about 4 million lead service lines nationwide, down from 9.2 million in its 2023 survey. They are concentrated in older cities, and no figure gives the share by build year.

check: Find where the water pipe enters the house, usually in the basement or crawl space near the meter.
Lead is dull gray and soft: scratch it gently with a coin or key and it shows shiny silver. A magnet will not stick, and joints often have a bulging 'wiped' shape.
Galvanized steel is gray but hard and magnetic; copper is the color of a penny.
Look up your address in the water utility's public service line inventory.
action: If you find lead, or the utility lists your line as lead or unknown, use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead for drinking and cooking water, and ask the utility about replacement programs. EPA puts full replacement at $1,200 to $12,300 per line, averaging $4,700. Replace the whole line, not just part of it.

sources.quote: With the latest data from 2025, EPA estimates that there are 4 million lead service lines across the country.
full LSLR can be expensive at an average cost of $4,700, ranging from $1,200 to $12,300 per line replaced
An estimated 4 million lead service lines (LSLs) serve water to properties in communities across the United States.
The Act prohibits the “use of any pipe, any pipe or plumbing fitting or fixture, any solder, or any flux, after June 1986, in the installation or repair of (i) any public water system
Lead pipes are more likely to be found in older cities and homes built before 1986.
Based on the findings from the 7th DWINSA, the total projected LSL in the United States is 9.2 million (see Exhibit 4). There are also an estimated 2.8 million standalone galvanized service lines.
Lead has not been used for water service piping since around 1950; lead contaminates potability.

caveat: Whether a given house has a lead line depends much more on the city than on the year: some places stopped by about 1950, while others kept using lead until the 1986 ban. EPA's national estimates have also changed sharply between surveys.

title: Lead solder in copper water pipes
hook: Copper water pipes installed before mid-1986 were commonly joined with lead solder, and EPA says solder and old brass fixtures are the most common lead source in homes without a lead service line.
summary: The 1986 Safe Drinking Water Act amendments banned solder with more than 0.2% lead in drinking-water plumbing after June 19, 1986, and gave states 24 months to enforce it. Faucets and fittings could still contain up to 8% lead until the limit dropped to a 0.25% weighted average in January 2014. You cannot reliably tell lead solder by eye; a water test is the practical check.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Tin-lead solder was the normal way to join copper pipe before the ban, but no survey counts how many pre-1986 houses still have those joints.

check: Look at exposed copper pipe joints in the basement, at the water heater or under sinks. Old lead solder is dull gray and lead-free solder is brighter silver, but age blurs the difference.
A lead swab test kit on a cleaned joint gives a better answer.
The most reliable check is a first-draw water test through your utility or a certified lab.
action: Test your water. If lead shows up, run the cold tap before drinking, use cold water for cooking, and use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead. Replacing old brass faucets with post-2014 ones helps; repiping for solder alone is rarely needed.

sources.publisher: US EPA (2015 public webinar summary and submitted comments on SDWA section 1417 regulations)
sources.quote: The main effect of this amendment, effective Jan. 4, 2014, will be to change the SDWA’s definition of lead free for pipes and pipe-fittings from “containing not more than 8.0 percent lead,”
At the time "lead free” was defined as solder and flux with no more than 0.2% lead and pipes with no more than 8%.
Among homes without lead service lines, the most common problem is with brass or chrome-plated brass faucets and plumbing with lead solder.
any solder, or any flux, after June 19, 1986, in the installa-
