sources.quote: With the latest data from 2025, EPA estimates that there are 4 million lead service lines across the country.
Lead pipes are more likely to be found in older cities and homes built before 1986.
Copper is the most common water service pipe material, and has been used since the 1930s.

caveat: The federal ban took effect in June 1986, but states had until June 1988 to enforce it, so houses built from 1986 to 1988 are a gray zone. Copper has been used since the 1930s, and many older houses have been partly or fully repiped.

title: Lochinvar, A. O. Smith and State condensing boilers (2020 recall)
hook: Some high-efficiency home boilers sold from 2016 to 2020 have a flue seal that can wear out and let carbon monoxide escape.
summary: About 34,300 condensing boilers, combi boilers and packaged systems sold from August 2016 to June 2020 under the Lochinvar, A. O. Smith and State Proline names were recalled. A flue grommet can deteriorate and let carbon monoxide escape. CPSC had 7 reports and 2 non-fatal CO injuries. A repair is the remedy.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 34,300 units were recalled in the US; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Check whether the boiler is branded Lochinvar, A. O. Smith or State Proline.
Find the rating plate on the outer jacket or the underside of the front panel, with the model and serial number.
The notice lists serial numbers 103475818 through 115078306 and model families such as ACB, KHB, SCB and WHL. Compare yours with the full list.
action: If it matches, contact the maker about the free repair described in the notice, and check the notice for whether it is still offered. Keep a working CO alarm near the boiler and bedrooms.

sources.quote: About 34,300 (In addition, about 3,642 units were sold in Canada)
from August 2016 through June 2020, for between $8,000 and $25,000, including installation

caveat: Boilers are replaced in older houses too, so the label matters more than build year. Later boiler recalls from other makers exist but were not checked for this guide.

title: LP Inner-Seal siding
hook: Louisiana-Pacific's Inner-Seal siding, marketed from 1985, swelled and rotted on enough houses to bring a class settlement covering everything installed before 1996.
summary: Inner-Seal is an oriented strand board (OSB) siding with a pressed wood-grain face. A federal class settlement covered siding installed before January 1, 1996, with claims due before January 1, 2003. Failing boards swell and crumble at the bottom edges, and rot can spread into the wall behind.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. The often-repeated figure of 800,000 homes could not be confirmed.

check: Look at a cut end or the bottom drip edge of the siding: visible wood flakes or strands mean OSB (hardboard shows uniform fiber instead).
Check bottom edges and around nail heads for swelling, crumbling and 'mushrooming'.
action: Keep paint and caulk intact, replace failed boards, and plan to re-side if damage is widespread. The settlement claim deadline passed in 2003, so no compensation remains.

sources.publisher: US District Court, D. Oregon, In re Louisiana-Pacific Inner-Seal Siding Litigation, Opinion and Order filed 26 July 2012 (govinfo)
sources.quote: Exterior Inner-Seal™ Siding has been installed prior to January 1, 1996
in 1985 began to market Inner-Seal siding for the exterior of homes

caveat: The 1985 start rests on a reference source. Many installs have already been replaced, and this was one brand among many sidings of the era.

title: Manufactured home built before 1994 wind standards
hook: After Hurricane Andrew, HUD raised the wind standards for manufactured homes made from July 13, 1994, with zones designed for 100 and 110 mph winds.
summary: Manufactured homes made before July 13, 1994 were built to the older wind standard. The newer rule created Wind Zones II and III for hurricane-prone areas. This matters only for manufactured homes, and most of all on the hurricane coast.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Every manufactured home made before the date was built to the older standard.

check: Find the data plate inside the home, often in a kitchen cabinet, the electrical panel or a bedroom closet.
Read the manufacture date and the wind-zone map showing which zone (I, II or III) the home was designed for.
No wind-zone designation, or a date before July 1994, means the older standard.
action: Have the anchoring and tie-downs checked and brought up to current installation standards. Only replacement gets you the post-1994 structural design.

sources.publisher: Federal Register, 59 FR (Jan 14, 1994), HUD final rule (GovInfo)
sources.quote: EFFECTIVE DATE: July 13, 1994, except that Secs. 3280.403(b) and (e) and 3280.404(b) and (e) will become effective January 17, 1995.

sources.publisher: Federal Register, HUD final rule, Jan 14, 1994 (GovInfo)
sources.quote: The design wind speeds for high wind areas are designated as 100 mph for Wind Zone II and 110 mph for Wind Zone III.

caveat: Date of manufacture governs, not the year the home was placed. Exactly which counties fall in each wind zone was not confirmed; the higher zones cover the hurricane coast.

title: Missing GFCI shock protection
hook: Houses built before 1973 had no GFCI shock protection at all, and the rules then added it one room at a time: bathrooms in 1975, garages in 1978, kitchens in 1987.
summary: A GFCI cuts the power in a fraction of a second when current leaks to ground, the kind of fault that electrocutes people near water. CPSC dates the requirements: outdoor outlets 1973, bathrooms 1975, garages 1978, some kitchen outlets 1987, unfinished basements and crawl spaces 1990. A house built before a given year was not required to have protection there unless it was added later.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists on how many older houses have had GFCIs added. CPSC notes that houses built before 1973 have no GFCI protection unless it was installed later.

check: Look for outlets with TEST and RESET buttons in bathrooms, at kitchen counters, in the garage, outdoors, in the basement and in the laundry.
Check the panel for breakers with a test button; a GFCI breaker protects a whole circuit.
One GFCI can protect ordinary-looking outlets further along the circuit: press TEST and see which outlets go dead.
Press RESET afterwards. GFCIs wear out, and older units can fail without any sign.
action: An electrician can add GFCI outlets or breakers where they are missing; they are allowed on ungrounded circuits too. Replace any GFCI that does not trip when tested.

sources.publisher: US CPSC Fact Sheet "What is a GFCI?"
sources.quote: Outdoors (since 1973)

GFCIs were first required in outdoor receptacle circuits in 1973, bathrooms in 1975, garage wall outlets in 1978, some kitchen receptacles since 1987, and all receptacle outlets in unfinished basements and crawl spaces since 1990.

Throughout the 1970s, GFCI installation requirements were gradually added for 120-volt receptacles in areas prone to possible water contact, including bathrooms, garages, and any receptacles located outdoors.

garages (1978), areas near hot tubs or spas (1981), hotel bathrooms (1984), kitchen counter sockets (1987), crawl spaces and unfinished basements (1990), near wet bar sinks (1993), near laundry sinks (2005)

caveat: These are national code edition years. States and cities adopted each edition anywhere from the same year to several years later, so a house built just after a milestone may not have that protection. Many older houses have had GFCIs added since, so build year is only a rough guide.

title: Missing or outdated smoke alarms
hook: Model building codes began requiring smoke alarms in every bedroom, linked so one sets off the rest, in 1988, so many older houses were built with far fewer.
summary: Smoke alarms went from 10% of US homes in 1975 to at least 92% by 2000, according to NIST. Codes then raised the bar: interconnected alarms in all sleeping rooms under the 1988 model codes, and alarms in all bedrooms under NFPA 72 from 1993. Alarms also wear out and should be replaced every 10 years.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of houses with alarms in every bedroom. NIST: the share of homes with at least one smoke alarm rose from 10% in 1975 to at least 92% by 2000.

check: Count them: one in each bedroom, one outside each sleeping area, and one on every level including the basement.
Press TEST on one: if all of them sound, they are interconnected.
Twist one off its base: a wiring plug behind it means hard-wired; none means battery-only.
Check the manufacture date on the back; over 10 years old means replace it.
action: Add alarms to every bedroom, hallway and level, using interconnected units; wireless interconnected alarms avoid new wiring. Replace any alarm over 10 years old. Many states also require working alarms at sale or rental.

sources.quote: Between 1975 and 2000, the share of homes with a smoke alarm rose from 10% to at least 92%
Between 1975 and 2000, the share of homes with a smoke alarm rose from 10% to at least 92%
Smoke alarms should be replaced when they fail to respond to testing, or every 10 years, whichever is sooner.
In 1988 BOCA, ICBO, and SBCCI model building codes begin requiring smoke alarms to be interconnected and located in all sleeping rooms.
In 1989 NFPA 74 first required smoke alarms to be interconnected in every new home construction, and 1993 NFPA 72 first required that smoke alarms be installed in all bedrooms.

caveat: The code dates come from reference sources and varied by code family and local adoption, so 1988 to 1993 is a transition and later is possible. Many older houses have been upgraded since.

title: No arc-fault (AFCI) breakers
hook: Arc-fault breakers, which detect the sparking that can start wiring fires, were first required in bedrooms of new houses in 2002.
summary: The 1999 National Electrical Code required AFCIs on bedroom circuits from 2002, for new construction only. Later editions widened the list: living areas, closets and hallways in 2008, kitchens and laundry areas in 2014. Houses built earlier usually have none, which matters most where wiring is old or damaged.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Houses built before about 2002 will lack AFCIs unless they were added later.

check: Open the panel door and look for breakers with a TEST button labeled AFCI, 'Arc Fault', 'Combination AFCI' or 'Dual Function'.
Ordinary breakers have no test button.
action: This is an optional upgrade: an electrician can fit AFCI or dual-function breakers where your panel supports them. They are not made for many older panels.

sources.publisher: US CPSC staff paper "New Technology for Preventing Residential Electrical Fires: Arc-Fault Circuit Interrupters (AFCIs)"
sources.quote: The 1999 National Electrical Code (NEC) requires AFCIs on bedroom branch circuits effective in the year 2002.
The 2014 NEC adds kitchens and laundry rooms to the list of rooms requiring AFCI circuitry, as well as any devices (such as lighting) requiring protection.

caveat: AFCI adoption was unusually uneven: several states delayed, limited or amended out the requirement, so build year is a weak guide on its own. Only the 2002 bedroom date is confirmed by a primary source.

title: Non-tempered glass in doors and showers
hook: Glass in doors, sliding patio doors and shower enclosures has had to be safety glass since July 1977, so older original glass may be ordinary glass that can cause serious cuts if someone falls through it.
summary: A federal CPSC standard made safety glazing mandatory from July 6, 1977 in doors, storm doors, sliding glass doors, and tub and shower doors and enclosures. A house built before then that still has its original glass in those places may have ordinary annealed glass. Building codes later added other locations near doors, floors, stairs and tubs.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of original pre-1977 glass still in place.

check: Look in each corner of the glass in doors, sliding doors and shower panels for a small etched or sandblasted mark naming the maker.
A mark reading 'tempered', '16 CFR 1201' or 'ANSI Z97.1' means safety glass.
No mark on a door or shower panel in an older house suggests ordinary glass.
action: Replace unmarked glass in doors and showers with tempered or laminated safety glass, starting with the places people are most likely to fall against.

sources.publisher: 16 CFR Part 1201 (2023 edition, via govinfo; ecfr.gov refuses automated requests)
sources.quote: The effective date of this part 1201 shall be July 6, 1977 except:

sources.publisher: Federal Register, 23 March 2016 (CPSC amendment notice, via govinfo)
sources.quote: On January 6, 1977 (42 FR 1427), as amended on June 20, 1977 (42 FR 31164), the Commission issued the Safety Standard for Architectural Glazing Materials
In the United States, federal law since 1977 has required safety glass located within doors and tub and shower enclosures.

caveat: Some states may have had their own safety-glazing laws earlier; that was not confirmed. Many doors and shower enclosures have been replaced since 1977.

title: Orangeburg sewer pipe
hook: After World War II, many houses were connected to the sewer with Orangeburg pipe, a tar-soaked fiber pipe that slowly deforms underground.
summary: Orangeburg is a bituminous fiber pipe used for house sewer lines from the postwar building boom until PVC and ABS replaced it in the 1970s. Over time it goes oval and blisters, causing backups. It also contains asbestos fibers, which matters when it is dug up.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Clay and cast iron were used in the same years, and not every house of the era got Orangeburg.

check: You cannot see it without digging; a sewer camera inspection by a plumber is the practical check.
On camera it shows as black pipe that has gone oval or blistered inside, in 8-foot lengths.
Symptoms: repeated backups, root clogs, or a sunken line across the lawn.
Your city or county sewer permit records sometimes name the pipe material.
action: Have a plumber run a camera down the line, especially before buying. If it is Orangeburg, plan to replace the line; lining works only while the pipe is still round.

sources.publisher: Wikipedia (article is tagged as needing more citations)
sources.quote: It was used from the 1860s through the 1970s, when it was replaced by PVC and ABS pipe for drain-waste-vent (DWV) applications.

caveat: Dates come from a reference article that is short on citations; the original maker closed by 1974, and others made similar pipe. Many houses of this era have clay or cast-iron sewer lines instead.

title: PCBs in old fluorescent light ballasts
hook: Fluorescent fixtures with magnetic ballasts made before 1979 may contain PCBs, and ballasts made after that without PCBs are labeled 'No PCBs'.
summary: EPA says PCB-containing building materials were used in buildings built or renovated between about 1950 and 1979, and that magnetic ballasts made before 1979 may contain PCBs. In a house the realistic case is an original fluorescent fixture in a garage, basement, kitchen or workshop. PCB caulk is documented mainly in schools and larger buildings.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists for houses; EPA's material is about schools and other larger buildings.

check: Turn the power off, open the fluorescent fixture cover and read the ballast label.
Ballasts marked 'No PCBs' were made after July 1, 1979.
An unlabeled magnetic ballast, or oily or tarry leakage, suggests a PCB ballast. Only magnetic T12 ballasts may contain PCBs.
action: Replace the old fixture or ballast, and take a PCB ballast to a hazardous-waste collection rather than the trash. Before renovating a 1950 to 1979 masonry apartment building, have suspect caulk tested.

sources.publisher: US EPA, PCBs in Building Materials
sources.quote: potential widespread use of PCB-containing building materials in schools and other buildings constructed or renovated between about 1950 and 1979

sources.publisher: US EPA, PCB-Containing Fluorescent Light Ballasts in School Buildings
sources.quote: EPA regulations also require that all FLBs built between July 1, 1979, and July 1, 1998, that do not contain PCBs must be labeled "No PCBs."

caveat: EPA's guidance addresses schools and other buildings, not single-family homes. Most original pre-1979 ballasts have long since been replaced.

title: Pella ProLine casement windows
hook: Pella ProLine aluminum-clad wood casement, awning and transom windows made from 1991 to 2009 were the subject of a class settlement over claims that water could get in and rot the wood.
summary: A federal class settlement, finally approved in 2019, covered ProLine casement, awning and transom windows made from January 1, 1991 to December 31, 2009. The claim was a design defect that let water get behind the aluminum cladding. Soft or stained wood at the bottom of the sash is the sign to look for.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. This is one product line from one maker.

check: Look for the Pella name etched in a corner of the glass or on the hardware.
These windows have aluminum cladding outside and wood inside.
Check the bottom of each sash for soft or stained wood.
action: Replace rotted sashes or whole units. The settlement's claim deadline could not be confirmed, so contact Pella or the settlement administrator to ask whether claims are still open.

sources.quote: manufactured by Pella Corporation between January 1, 1991 and December 31, 2009

sources.publisher: US Court of Appeals, 7th Circuit, Eubank v. Pella Corp., Nos. 13-2091 et al., decided 2 June 2014 (govinfo)
sources.quote: manufactured and sold between 1991 and 2006 had a design defect that allowed water to enter behind the

caveat: Only casement, awning and transom windows in this line were covered. Windows are often replaced, so these can also turn up in older houses.

title: Plexvent and Ultravent plastic flue pipe
hook: About 250,000 gas furnaces and boilers were vented through gray or black plastic pipe printed Plexvent or Ultravent, which was recalled because joints can crack or separate and leak carbon monoxide.
summary: In 1998 CPSC announced a program to replace this high-temperature plastic vent (HTPV) pipe free of charge on about 250,000 systems; about 93,000 had been replaced by October 2005. The danger is carbon monoxide escaping from cracked or separated joints. CPSC gives dates only for a subset on Goodman furnaces, made October 1988 to July 1994.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC: about 250,000 systems nationally, about 93,000 of them replaced by October 2005.

check: Follow the flue pipe from the furnace or boiler to where it leaves the house, usually through a side wall.
Gray or black plastic pipe printed 'Plexvent', 'Plexvent II' or 'Ultravent' is the recalled type.
White PVC or CPVC pipe is not part of the recall.
action: Have a heating contractor inspect it promptly. At this age, replacing the vent along with the appliance is often the realistic fix. Whether any recall remedy is still honored is unknown.

This program will replace, free of charge, an estimated 250,000 HTPV pipe systems attached to gas or propane furnaces or boilers in consumers' homes.
The program's purpose is to replace, free of charge, an estimated 250,000 HTPV pipe systems attached to gas or propane furnaces or boilers in consumers' homes.
About 93,000 HTPV pipes have been replaced as of October 1, 2005.

caveat: The full date range of these vents was never published; 1988 to 1994 comes from one subset. Many have already been replaced along with their furnaces.

title: Polybutylene water pipes
hook: Gray plastic polybutylene pipe, stamped PB2110, went into houses from 1978 to the mid-1990s, and its failures led to a class action settled for about $1 billion.
summary: Polybutylene was made for home plumbing from 1978 until mid-1995, and its leaks led to the Cox v. Shell Oil class action. InterNACHI notes that owners can face higher insurance premiums or be refused coverage.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: InterNACHI gives an upper estimate of up to 10 million homes. Against the tens of millions of homes built from 1978 to 1995, that is a minority of houses of the era.

check: Look at the pipes entering the water heater, under sinks, at the main shut-off and at the meter.
Polybutylene is flexible, 1/2 to 1 inch across, usually gray (sometimes blue outdoors, black or silver), and stamped 'PB2110'.
Fittings are gray or white plastic, or copper or brass with aluminum or copper crimp rings.
Do not confuse it with PEX (white, red or blue, stamped PEX) or CPVC (rigid and cream-colored).
action: Talk to a plumber about repiping in PEX or copper, the standard recommendation. The settlement money is no longer available. Check with your insurer, since some charge more or decline coverage.

sources.quote: Polybutylene (PB) was a plastic manufactured between 1978 and mid-1995 for use as piping in home plumbing systems.
Polybutylene plumbing (marketed as Poly-B ) was used in several million homes built in the United States and Canada from around 1978 to 1997.

caveat: Sources put the end anywhere from mid-1995 to 1997, so a few later houses are possible. Most houses of the era have copper or other plastic pipe, and many polybutylene systems have already been replaced.

title: Mobile home built before the HUD Code
hook: Mobile homes made before June 15, 1976 predate the federal HUD Code and cannot get FHA-insured mortgages.
summary: Every manufactured home built after June 15, 1976 carries a HUD certification label and meets federal construction and safety standards. Earlier units were built before those standards, and HUD does not issue labels for them. This matters only if your home is a manufactured (mobile) home.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of surviving pre-1976 units. Every mobile home made before the date predates the HUD Code by definition.

check: Look for a metal certification label, about 2 by 4 inches, riveted to the outside at the tail end of each section.
Look for a paper data plate inside, often in a kitchen cabinet, the electrical panel or a bedroom closet, giving the manufacture date.
No label and no data plate, plus a title showing a pre-1976 year, means pre-HUD Code.
action: It cannot be certified after the fact. Focus on safety upgrades such as smoke alarms, a wiring evaluation and tie-downs. Expect financing limits: FHA does not insure mortgages on these homes.

sources.publisher: HUD Office of Manufactured Housing Programs (labels page)
sources.quote: If the certification label (also known as a HUD tag) is missing from a home, the Department does not reissue labels for manufactured homes.
be constructed after June 15, 1976, in conformance with the Federal Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards, as evidenced by an affixed certification label
manufactured homes produced prior to that date are ineligible for insured financing
The Federal Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards (commonly known as the HUD Code) went into effect June 15, 1976.

caveat: The date is when the home left the factory, not its model year or when it was placed, so a '1976' home can fall on either side.

title: Problem drywall (Chinese drywall)
hook: Some houses built or renovated from 2001 to 2009, mostly in Florida and the Gulf states, got imported drywall that gives off sulfur gases and blackens copper.
summary: CPSC has about 4,051 reports of problem drywall from 44 states, and early reports came overwhelmingly from Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Virginia. The gases corrode air-conditioner coils, wiring and gas fittings. Federal remediation guidance amounts to a gut renovation: remove the drywall and replace wiring components, alarms and some gas piping.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC has about 4,051 reports. In March 2010, over 90% came from Florida (59%), Louisiana (20%), Mississippi (6%), Alabama (5%) and Virginia (4%). Even there it is a small share of houses built in these years.

check: Look at the copper tubing on the air conditioner's indoor coil: blackened copper, not green, is CPSC's warning sign. An electrician can check the bare ground wires in outlet and switch boxes for the same thing.
Note any sulfur or rotten-egg smell, or repeated air-conditioner coil failures.
In the attic, look at the back of exposed drywall for Chinese manufacturer markings such as 'Knauf Tianjin'.
A lab test of the drywall or the copper corrosion confirms it.
action: If the signs line up, follow CPSC and HUD's identification and remediation guidance and get a specialist inspection. A Senate hearing record described the Louisiana court remediation protocol at about $86 per square foot, more than $200,000 for a 2,400-square-foot home. No open settlement program was found.

sources.quote: (if drywall was installed between 2005 and 2009, must have at least two of the below. For installations between 2001 and 2004, at least four of the following conditions must be met:)
the CPSC has received about 4,051 reports from residents in 44 states, the District of Columbia, American Samoa, and Puerto Rico
More than 90% of reports are from Florida (59%), Louisiana (20%), Mississippi (6%) and Alabama (5%) and Virginia (4%).

sources.publisher: US Senate hearing record, S. Hrg. 112-348 (December 6, 2011)
sources.quote: pegged at $86 per square foot. That would amount to more than $200,000 for a 2,400 square foot home
Sources estimated that from 60,000 to 100,000 homes could be affected.

caveat: CPSC asks for more corroborating evidence for 2001 to 2004 installs than for 2005 to 2009, which shows where the problem concentrates. Renovations in this period could have brought it into older houses, and reports came from 44 states, not only the five listed.

title: Crumbling concrete foundations (pyrrhotite)
hook: In parts of north-central Connecticut and central Massachusetts, some foundations poured with local quarry stone are crumbling because of a mineral called pyrrhotite.
summary: NIST says damage to concrete in central Connecticut has been attributed to pyrrhotite, an iron sulfide mineral in the aggregate. State officials use 1983 to 2015 as the window for affected foundations, and cracking usually appears 10 to 30 years after construction. The fix is replacing the foundation, which is a major job.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Estimates of affected homes vary by two orders of magnitude, and the risk is limited to certain towns; outside them it is essentially nil.

check: In the basement, look at the foundation walls for horizontal cracks and map-pattern (spider-web) cracking.
Look for white powdery deposits, rust-brown staining and flaking.
A clean-looking wall does not rule it out; a licensed engineer's visual inspection and a core sample tested for pyrrhotite confirm it.
action: If you are in an affected town, have a licensed engineer inspect the foundation, especially before buying. Connecticut and Massachusetts have run programs for testing, and Connecticut for repairs; check what is currently available.

sources.quote: Damage to concrete structures in residential and commercial construction in central Connecticut have been attributed to the iron sulfide mineral pyrrhotite.
Pyrrhotite has been linked to crumbling concrete basements in Quebec , Massachusetts and Connecticut where local quarries extracted insufficiently characterised aggregates for making concrete.

caveat: The 1983 to 2015 window comes from state officials' figures that could not be independently confirmed, and only towns near the source quarries are affected. Most houses in Connecticut and Massachusetts are not at risk.

title: R-22 (Freon) air conditioner
hook: New air conditioners could not be built to use R-22 from 2010, and US production of the refrigerant ended in 2020.
summary: Air conditioners and heat pumps made before January 1, 2010 commonly use R-22 (HCFC-22). EPA says you can keep running one as long as you like, but with R-22 no longer produced, a leak can make repair uneconomic. Replacing it usually means a new outdoor unit and indoor coil together.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of pre-2010 units still in service.

check: Read the data plate on the outdoor unit: 'R-22' or 'HCFC-22' means the old refrigerant; newer units say R-410A, R-454B or R-32.
The manufacture date is usually on the same plate.
action: Nothing to do while it works. Budget for replacing the outdoor unit and indoor coil together when it fails.

sources.quote: U.S. production and import of HCFC-22 ended on January 1, 2020, but you may continue to use HCFC-22 in your existing system for as long as necessary.
Ban on production, import and use of HCFC-22 and HCFC-142b except for on-going servicing needs of existing equipment

sources.publisher: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances
sources.quote: No production or import of HCFC-142b and HCFC-22, except for use in equipment manufactured before January 1, 2010

sources.publisher: US EPA, Homeowners and Consumers FAQ
sources.quote: You can no longer purchase a central AC unit that uses HCFC-22.

caveat: Air conditioning is often added or replaced long after a house is built, so the unit's age matters far more than the house's.

title: R-410A air conditioners and heat pumps
hook: Central AC installed from about 2010 to 2025 most likely runs on R-410A, the refrigerant new equipment is now moving away from.
summary: R-410A replaced R-22 in new central air conditioners and heat pumps. From January 1, 2025, EPA restricts making or importing new home systems that use high-warming refrigerants, so new equipment is moving to alternatives. Existing R-410A systems can keep running and be serviced.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: New equipment could no longer use R-22 from 2010 (EPA), and R-410A was the main replacement. No count of homes exists; this is an inference.

check: Find the nameplate on the outdoor unit.
Look for the refrigerant listed: R-410A, R-22, or a newer type such as R-454B or R-32.
action: Nothing is required for a working system. When it is time to replace it, ask the contractor which refrigerant the new system uses and whether any other parts need changing.

sources.quote: portable room air conditioning) 700 January 1, 2025
No installation compliance date for systems where all specified components were manufactured or imported prior to January 1, 2025.

caveat: The 2010 start is approximate. EPA has since changed some installation dates for equipment made before 2025, so check EPA's current page before relying on a cutoff. Many older houses got an R-410A system as a replacement.

title: Recalled LP composite decking
hook: About 48 million linear feet of LP WeatherBest, ABTCo and Veranda composite decking sold from 2005 to 2008 was recalled because boards could break underfoot.
summary: In May 2009, CPSC announced Louisiana-Pacific's recall of composite decking and railing sold from January 2005 to August 2008, after 37 reports of breakage and 14 injuries. LP offered free inspection and replacement. Separately, Trex settled a class action over surface flaking and mold spotting on early boards.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC: about 48 million linear feet recalled. Composite was a minority of decks built in these years.

check: Look at the deck boards: uncapped composite is the same color and texture all the way through, with no plastic shell.
Recalled LP boards may be soft, swollen, flaking or cracked, especially in damp shade.
Look for a brand name printed on the underside or end of a board.
action: Check CPSC recall 09-217 and contact Louisiana-Pacific about the free inspection and replacement; it was not confirmed whether that remedy is still honored. Replace any soft or cracked boards.

sources.publisher: US Consumer Product Safety Commission, recall 09-217 (13 May 2009)
sources.quote: nationwide from January 2005 to August 2008

sources.publisher: US District Court, N.D. California, Ross v. Trex Co., Order granting preliminary approval of settlement, filed 30 July 2009 (govinfo)
sources.quote: types of defects: “surface flaking” and “mold spotting.”

caveat: These are sale dates, and decks are often added long after a house is built, so build year predicts this poorly. Most decks of this period are wood or other brands.

title: Rheem and Paloma power-vent tankless water heaters (2007 recall)
hook: A batch of gas tankless water heaters sold from 2004 to 2006 could build up dust and produce carbon monoxide.
summary: About 42,200 Rheem and Paloma power-vent tankless gas water heaters sold from May 2004 to December 2006 were recalled for repair in 2007. A misplaced filter-door switch could let dust build up, creating a carbon monoxide risk.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 42,200 units were recalled, and tankless heaters were a small share of water heaters then; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Check whether the water heater is a wall-mounted tankless unit branded Rheem or Paloma.
Read the model number on its label and compare it with the list on the CPSC notice.
Check that the air filter door is in place.
action: If it matches, contact the installer or Rheem about the repair described in the notice, and check the notice for current details. Keep a working CO alarm nearby.

sources.quote: About 42,200
May 2004 through December 2006 for between $800 and $1,300

caveat: Tankless heaters are often fitted when an older tank fails, so they turn up in houses of any age.

title: Rinnai EnergySaver wall furnaces (2008 recall)
hook: Some Rinnai direct-vent wall heaters made from 2000 to 2007 have a gasket that can fail and leak carbon monoxide.
summary: Rinnai recalled about 52,000 EnergySaver direct-vent wall furnaces, models RHFE-431 and RHFE-556, made from February 2000 to December 2007. A gasket can fail and let carbon monoxide into the home. The notice offered a free repair kit.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 52,000 units were recalled, and wall furnaces are a minority heating type; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Look for a Rinnai heater mounted on an outside wall with its vent going straight through the wall.
Find the rating plate on the right side of the unit; the model number is at the top.
Look for RHFE-431 or RHFE-556 (with FAIII, WTA or WTA-72B/76B suffixes).
The first four digits of the serial number, at the bottom of the plate, are the year and month made: 0002 through 0712 are in the recall window.
action: If it matches, contact Rinnai about the free repair kit using the details on the recall notice, and check the notice for whether it is still offered. Make sure there is a working CO alarm nearby.

sources.quote: The recall includes only those units manufactured from February 2000 through December 2007.
About 52,000

caveat: Wall heaters are often added to older houses and additions, so build year is a weak guide here. The rating plate is what tells you.

title: Siemens and Murray circuit breakers (2010 recall)
hook: Siemens and Murray breakers sold in the summer of 2010 have a clip that can break and let the panel overheat.
summary: Siemens recalled about 2.2 million breakers, load centers and meter combos sold from June to August 2010 under the Siemens and Murray names. A spring clip can break in normal use, loosening the connection and risking overheating, arcing and fire in the panel. The 2010 notice offered a free electrician inspection and replacement.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 2.2 million units were recalled, counting breakers, load centers and meter combos together; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Open the panel door (not the cover behind it) and read the brand on the label and the breakers: Siemens or Murray.
If it is one of those and the house was built or re-paneled around 2010, note it.
Leave the date-code check to an electrician: the codes are on the side of the breaker, behind the panel cover.
action: Do not remove the panel cover yourself. Ask an electrician to compare the breakers with the CPSC list, and contact Siemens about the free inspection and replacement; check the recall notice for whether it is still offered.

sources.quote: The recalled circuit breakers have a spring clip that can break during normal use
About 2.2 million
from June 2010 through August 2010 for between $2.50 to $235

caveat: The sale window was only three months, so most Siemens and Murray panels are not affected. Panels replaced in older houses in 2010 can have them too.

title: Split-bus panels with no main breaker
hook: Between the 1950s and the mid-1980s, many houses got a split-bus panel, which has no single main breaker: shutting off all the power can take up to six switches.
summary: A split-bus panel puts up to six large breakers in an upper group, one of which feeds a lower group of smaller breakers. Existing ones are allowed to stay, but there is no one-switch shutoff in an emergency and the panels are now decades old. Since the 2020 National Electrical Code, new services must have one main disconnect.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Most manufacturers offered this style, but its share of houses of the era is unknown.

check: Open the panel door: there is no single large breaker marked 'Main'.
Instead you see a top group of up to six double-pole breakers, one often labeled 'Lighting Main' or 'Sub Main', and a separate lower group of single-pole breakers.
Read the brand on the label too: some split-bus panels are Federal Pacific or Zinsco.
action: Make sure the breakers that shut off the house are clearly labeled. Have an electrician inspect it, and plan to replace it with a main-breaker panel when its condition calls for it or you add big loads such as an EV charger or heat pump.

sources.quote: Between the 1950s and mid-1980s, split bus panels were installed in many homes. These panels do not have a main breaker or one main disconnect.

caveat: The end date comes from one trade source ('mid-1980s'); the claim that a 1981 code change ended the design was not confirmed. Many of these panels have already been replaced.

title: Square D arc-fault (AFCI) breakers (2004 recall)
hook: Some Square D arc-fault breakers from 2004, the ones with a blue test button, may not catch the sparking they were installed to catch.
summary: About 700,000 Square D QO and Homeline arc-fault breakers made after March 1, 2004 and sold from March to September 2004 were recalled because they can fail to detect an arc fault. They still work as ordinary breakers. They were put in to meet the 2002 electrical code rule for bedroom circuits.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: About 700,000 units were recalled; no count of affected homes exists.

check: Open the panel door and look for Square D QO or Homeline breakers marked AFCI or arc fault, usually on bedroom circuits.
Note whether the test button is blue.
Have an electrician read the date code stamped in red on the breaker label: CN, DN, EN, FN, GN, HN or JN are the recalled codes.
action: If they match, contact Schneider Electric (Square D) about replacement, and check the recall notice for current details.

sources.quote: The recalled units were manufactured after March 1, 2004, and have a blue test button.
About 700,000
They are required to be installed in bedroom circuits in accordance with the 2002 National Electrical Code.

caveat: Only a seven-month batch is affected. A house built in 2004 or 2005 is the likeliest place to find one, but a breaker could have been added later.

title: Square D QO Plug-On Neutral panel recall
hook: About 1.4 million Square D QO Plug-On Neutral panels made between February 2020 and January 2022 were recalled for an overheating and fire hazard.
summary: In June 2022, CPSC announced the recall of Square D QO Plug-On Neutral load centers made February 2020 through January 2022, date codes 200561 to 220233. At the time the firm had one report of a loose wire and no injuries. The remedy offered was a free inspection and repair or replacement.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: CPSC: about 1.4 million units in the US. No figure gives the share of houses built in these years.

check: Open the panel door and look for 'Square D', 'QO' and 'Plug-On Neutral' on the label.
Find the catalog number and date code on the label inside the door; recalled units have date codes from 200561 to 220233.
Compare with the recall notice, or call Schneider Electric at 888-778-2733.
action: If yours is in the recall range, contact Schneider Electric for the free inspection and repair or replacement under CPSC recall 22-159. It was not confirmed whether the program is still running, so call to check.

sources.quote: The recalled circuit breaker boxes were manufactured between February 2020 and January 2022, with date codes between 200561 and 220233.

caveat: The recall also covers panels installed as replacements in older houses, so build year is only a rough guide. Houses finished in 2022 and 2023 may have panels from late in the window. Most houses built in these years have other brands or models.

title: Synthetic stucco (barrier EIFS)
hook: Synthetic stucco over wood framing sounds hollow when you knock on it, and the early 'barrier' kind could trap water and rot the wall behind.
summary: EIFS is foam board with a thin stucco-like finish. Leak problems showed up from the late 1980s, and building standards moved houses to drainable EIFS with a drainage cavity. In 1997 EIFS was about 4% of the residential siding market.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: EIFS was about 4% of the US residential siding market in 1997 (Wikipedia, citing a trade source).

check: Knock on or press the wall: synthetic stucco sounds hollow and gives slightly, while traditional stucco is hard.
Look for foam showing at a damaged spot or at the bottom edge, and for finish running right down to or below the ground.
Look for staining below window corners and where decks or roofs meet the wall.
action: Before buying, or if you see stains, get a moisture-probe inspection by a certified EIFS inspector. Dry walls may need only flashing and sealant work; wet walls may need stripping and re-cladding with a drained system.

sources.quote: It has been in use in Europe since the 1950s, and in the U.S. since the late ‘60s. It is often used on wood-framed houses.

sources.publisher: InterNACHI, How to Inspect for Moisture Intrusion (2012)
sources.quote: building standards only allow the use of a new type of drainable EIFS (i.e., drained cavity) on residential construction
As of 1997 EIFS accounted for about 4% of the residential siding market and 12% of the commercial siding market.

sources.publisher: Wikipedia, Exterior insulation finishing system (second excerpt)
sources.quote: In the late 1980s problems started developing due to water leakage in EIFS-clad buildings.

caveat: Start and end years are approximate; barrier EIFS was never banned nationally and continued in some places into the early 2000s. It is reported to be most common on mid- and upper-priced houses in parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.

title: Outlets without child-safety shutters
hook: Since the 2008 electrical code, new houses get outlets with built-in shutters that stop a child pushing a key or hairpin into the slot.
summary: Tamper-resistant outlets have spring-loaded shutters that open only when both prongs of a plug push in together. They were first required by the 2008 National Electrical Code, and by 2016 that applied to new houses in all but five states. A figure cited by the electrical manufacturers' association and InterNACHI is about 2,400 children a year hurt by pushing objects into outlets.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Houses built before their state adopted the 2008 code will generally lack them unless outlets were replaced.

check: Look closely at an outlet: 'TR' embossed on the face between the slots means tamper-resistant.
You can see plastic shutters inside the slots.
action: If small children live in or visit the house, have outlets replaced with TR-listed ones. Current code requires a TR outlet whenever one is replaced anyway, and they cost little more than standard ones.

sources.publisher: HUD Manufactured Housing Consensus Committee, draft meeting minutes October 2016 (the statement is in a NEMA comment letter reproduced in the minutes, not a HUD finding)
sources.quote: TRRs have been required since the 2008 edition of the NEC, which means that they are required for new homes in all but five states.
approximately 2,400 children suffer from electrical shock and burns in the home each year when they force foreign objects into unprotected electrical outlets
Starting with the 2008 National Electrical Code

caveat: 2008 is the model code year; states adopted it at different times. The rule did not cover manufactured homes.

title: Two-prong outlets with no ground
hook: Outlets with only two slots were normal until 1962, when grounded outlets became required in new houses.
summary: Before the early 1960s, house circuits usually had two wires and no ground. Three-prong appliances and surge protectors rely on a ground, and plug adapters defeat that protection. One reference source dates the rule for every new outlet later still, to January 1, 1974.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Before 1962 the code did not require grounded outlets, so a house of that age started with mostly two-wire circuits; how many have been rewired is unknown.

check: Look at the outlets: two slots and no round ground hole means an ungrounded outlet.
Where an older house has three-prong outlets, a plug-in outlet tester from a hardware store will show 'open ground' if no ground is connected.
At the panel, look for old cables with only two conductors and no bare wire.
action: An electrician can run new grounded circuits, or protect ungrounded outlets with GFCI devices labeled 'No Equipment Ground', an accepted fix according to InterNACHI. A GFCI gives shock protection but is not a true ground.

sources.quote: an important safety feature that has been required in new construction since 1962
1-15R receptacles have been prohibited in new construction in the United States and Canada since 1962, but remain in many older buildings

caveat: 1962 is the year trade and reference sources give for new construction; the 1974 date and local adoption lag mean some later houses may have two-wire circuits too. Many older houses have been partly rewired, or had three-prong outlets swapped in with no ground behind them.

title: Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI)
hook: About 500,000 homes had foam insulation pumped into their walls in the 1970s, and CPSC banned it in 1982 before a court overturned the ban.
summary: Urea-formaldehyde foam was injected into wall cavities, mostly as a retrofit in existing houses during the 1970s energy crisis. CPSC banned it for homes in 1982; a federal appeals court overturned the ban in 1983, and little was installed after that. Its formaldehyde release fades within years, so today it is mostly a disclosure and resale question.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC's 1982 release referred to some 500,000 homes already insulated with the foam, a small share of US housing.

check: Look on the outside walls for rows of patched 1- to 2-inch plugs in siding or mortar joints, where foam was injected.
In the basement at the sill, or behind an outlet cover on an outside wall (power off first), look for dry, crumbly, off-white to tan foam that powders when touched.
action: Usually nothing needs doing. If anyone has symptoms, an indoor air test for formaldehyde is the next step. Removal means opening the walls and is rarely justified on health grounds. Some state disclosure forms ask about UFFI, so keep a note.

sources.quote: has banned the sale of urea formaldehyde foam insulation for use in residences and schools

sources.publisher: US CPSC news release, March 1, 1982 (dissenting commissioner's statement)
sources.quote: avoiding the substantial lowering of resale values of some 500,000 homes already insulated with U.F. foam which could result from a ban
was lifted yesterday when the Solicitor General's office decided not to appeal the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals' ruling which had overturned the ban

sources.publisher: US CPSC news release, October 21, 1983 (URL path says 1984)
sources.quote: still considers urea formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI) to be a hazardous product
UFFI is generally found in homes built or retrofitted from the 1930s to the 1970s, often in basements, wall cavities, crawl spaces and attics.

caveat: It was mostly added to existing houses, so a 1920s house is as likely to have it as a 1975 one. The start and peak years are approximate.

title: Yellow CSST gas tubing without bonding
hook: Flexible yellow stainless-steel gas tubing can be damaged by a nearby lightning strike, and older installs often lack the bonding wire that reduces the risk.
summary: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) in a yellow jacket came into use in houses around 1990. A class action against its makers covered tubing installed in homes as of September 5, 2006, and bonding the tubing to the electrical ground is now standard. Houses built before bonding became routine may not have it.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. It applies only to houses with gas service.

check: Look at exposed gas piping in the basement, attic, crawl space or at the furnace and water heater: flexible corrugated tubing in a yellow jacket is CSST (black-jacketed tubing is a newer type).
Look for bonding: a clamp on a rigid gas fitting with a bare or green copper wire running to the electrical panel or grounding system.
action: If you have yellow CSST and see no bonding wire, have a licensed electrician bond it following the tubing maker's instructions and current code. It is a small job.

sources.quote: class-action lawsuit against manufacturers of CCST (Titeflex, Ward, OmegaFlex and Parker Hannifin) installed in homes as of September 5, 2006

sources.publisher: Wikipedia, Corrugated stainless steel tubing (article lacks inline citations)
sources.quote: Yellow-jacketed CSST should be bonded (connected to the electrical service panel's ground bus) at its entrance into a building. Many local codes require this.

caveat: The start year and the code year that made bonding mandatory (reported as 2009) were not confirmed, and states adopted codes at different times. CSST is still installed today, with bonding.

title: Uncoated brass gas appliance connectors
hook: Old flexible brass gas connectors behind stoves, dryers and water heaters can crack, and CPSC linked them to 35 deaths.
summary: CPSC warned in 1996 that uncoated brass connectors, not made for at least the previous 10 years, can crack or break, citing 200 failures associated with 35 deaths and 59 injuries. A connector is usually replaced along with its appliance, so they survive mainly with very old gas appliances. Modern connectors are stainless steel or plastic-coated.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Connectors are usually replaced with the appliance.

check: CPSC says not to move a gas appliance to look; check only where the connector is already visible.
An old connector is a dull brass-colored corrugated tube with no gray or yellow plastic coating.
Modern connectors are stainless steel or coated.
action: Have a qualified gas technician check the connectors on older appliances and replace any uncoated brass one. A connector should never be reused.

sources.quote: older, uncoated, brass connectors, which have not been made for at least the past 10 years
These gas connectors are made of brass, are uncoated, and can crack or break

caveat: CPSC gave no exact year manufacture stopped, only 'at least the past 10 years' as of 1996. The age of the appliance matters more than the age of the house.

title: Unlined masonry chimney
hook: Many chimneys built before the 1950s have no flue liner, just bare brick, which can let a chimney fire or carbon monoxide reach the house.
summary: Since the 1950s, building codes in many places have required new chimneys to have a flue liner, usually square clay tiles. Older chimneys may have none, and lined chimneys of any age can have cracked tiles. A chimney inspection is the way to know.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Sources say only that pre-1950s houses 'often' have unlined chimneys.

check: With the fire out and cold, look up from the fireplace or down from the clean-out with a flashlight.
Bare brick and mortar means unlined; square orange or buff clay tiles mean lined.
Cracked tiles usually need a camera inspection (an NFPA 211 Level 2 inspection).
action: Have a certified chimney sweep inspect it before using the fireplace or connecting an appliance. Fixes include a stainless-steel or cast-in-place liner, new tiles, or closing off the flue.

sources.publisher: InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart
sources.quote: Chimney Flue Tile 40 to 120
Since the 1950s, building codes in many locations require newly built chimneys to have a flue liner.

caveat: There is no single national date; liner rules came in locally and gradually from about the 1950s. Many older chimneys have been relined since.

title: Unreinforced brick (URM) houses
hook: Along Utah's Wasatch Front, many solid-brick houses built before 1975 have no steel reinforcement, and FEMA counts over 185,000 such buildings in the Salt Lake Valley alone.
summary: Unreinforced masonry walls can crack and fall in an earthquake, and parapets and chimneys tend to go first. In Utah, codes for new buildings began addressing this in 1975, and many unreinforced buildings there are single-family houses. Tying walls to floors and roof and bracing chimneys are the usual retrofits.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: FEMA P-774: over 185,000 unreinforced masonry buildings in the Salt Lake Valley alone, many of them single-family homes.

check: Look at the outside brick walls: a row of bricks laid end-on (a header course) every 5 to 7 rows means solid brick, not veneer.
At a window opening, walls 8 to 13 inches thick point to solid masonry.
Star-shaped or square metal plates on the outside wall show past retrofit ties.
Brick veneer over a wood frame has no header rows and is a different, lesser issue.
action: Have a structural engineer assess it. Salt Lake City has run a 'Fix the Bricks' program that helps pay for roof-to-wall ties and chimney bracing; check whether it covers your house.

sources.quote: Buildings built after 1975, when codes for new buildings began to address this seismic vulnerability in Utah, are exempt.
In the Salt Lake Valley alone, there are over 185,000 unreinforced masonry buildings, many of them single-family residences

By the time when American building codes started to include seismic requirements, first in California in the 1930s and slowly spreading nationwide, reinforced masonry construction techniques became increasingly standard.
over 98 percent of the 25,900 URM buildings now in loss reduction programs. But so far, only about 70 percent of the owners have reduced earthquake risk by retrofitting

the 1933 Long Beach earthquake resulted in a near-immediate statewide ban on construction of new unreinforced masonry school buildings and the Field Act . A State law enacted in 1986 required seismic retrofitting of existing structures.

caveat: Shown for Utah, where the 1975 date is confirmed. California, Oregon and Washington also have unreinforced brick buildings with earlier cutoffs (California's seismic codes began in the 1930s), but most of those are commercial or apartment buildings.

title: Vermiculite attic insulation
hook: Loose, pebbly vermiculite insulation in the attic, much of it sold as Zonolite, may contain asbestos, and EPA advises treating it as if it does.
summary: A mine near Libby, Montana, supplied over 70% of US vermiculite from 1919 to 1990, and its ore was contaminated with asbestos. The insulation was often poured into the attics of existing houses, so any house standing before about 1990 could have it. It is a risk mainly when disturbed by attic storage, wiring or remodeling.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Wikipedia reports a US government estimate that vermiculite was used in more than 35 million homes; other estimates are far lower. Even the high figure is a minority of houses.

check: Look into the attic from the hatch without stepping in or disturbing anything.
Vermiculite is loose, lightweight granules about 1/8 to 1/2 inch, shiny and accordion-like, gray-brown to silver-gold, lying between the joists.
It is often under newer fiberglass or cellulose; empty Zonolite bags are sometimes left in the attic.
EPA advises against relying on a negative lab test.
action: Do not disturb it, and keep stored belongings out of that attic. Sealing gaps around ceiling lights and openings helps keep dust out of the house. For any attic work, hire a licensed asbestos abatement contractor. The Zonolite Attic Insulation Trust has reimbursed part of removal costs for confirmed Zonolite; check whether it is still accepting claims.

sources.publisher: US EPA, Protect Your Family from Asbestos-Contaminated Vermiculite Insulation
sources.quote: A mine near Libby, Montana, was the source of over 70 percent of all vermiculite sold in the United States from 1919 to 1990.
the mine continued to operate until stiffer environmental controls finally forced it to close in 1990
The United States government estimates that vermiculite was used in more than 35 million homes, but does not recommend its removal.

caveat: This was largely a do-it-yourself product added to existing houses, so build year is a weak guide. Most houses do not have it, and estimates of how many do disagree widely.

title: Zinsco and Sylvania-Zinsco panels
hook: Zinsco panels, made from 1943 until about 1981 and later sold under the Sylvania name, have narrow breakers with brightly colored tips, and inspectors treat them as a problem panel.
summary: Zinsco made panels from 1943, sold the business to GTE-Sylvania in 1973, and production of Zinsco-design panels ended around 1981. InterNACHI says these panels have a reputation for being problematic and recommends evaluation by an electrician. The aluminum bus bars tied to the failures came in during the early 1960s.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Trade sources say they were most common in the West, but no figure backs that.

check: Open the panel door and read the label for Zinsco, Sylvania, Sylvania-Zinsco, GTE-Sylvania or Kearney.
The breakers are distinctive: narrow, with brightly colored handle tips (red, blue, green or yellow), clipped onto vertical bus bars.
action: Have a licensed electrician evaluate the panel. Replacing the whole panel is the usual fix, because new breakers do not change the bus design.

sources.quote: These panels have a reputation for being problematic and further evaluation by a qualified electrician is recommended.
In 1973, Martin Zinsmeyer sold the Zinsco Electric Company to GTE-Sylvania. During that ownership, the product line remained the same, with new labeling and branding

caveat: The dates rest mainly on one reference article, and the failure rates that circulate come from non-government testing. Plenty of these panels are still working, but InterNACHI treats the brand as one to have checked.
